learn from specific types of noisy feedback, but across teachers and tasks
different forms of feedback may be required. Instead we propose that in order
to learn from a diversity of scenarios we need to learn from a variety of
feedback. To learn from a variety of feedback we make the following insight:
the teacher's cost function is latent and we can model a stream of feedback as
a stream of loss functions. We then use any online learning algorithm to
minimize the sum of these losses. With this insight we can learn from a
diversity of feedback that is weakly correlated with the teacher's true cost
function. We unify prior work into a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm
and show that regardless of feedback we can obtain the same regret bounds. We
demonstrate our approach by learning to perform a household navigation task on
a robotic racecar platform. Our results show that our approach can learn from
a variety of feedback including reward feedback that is noisy in the
continuum.

the applied gate voltage is varied. While the observations are qualitatively as
expected for quantum interference between coherent quantum phase slip elements,
the period of the tuning is orders of magnitude larger than expected on the
basis of simple capacitance considerations.
  From the tuning characteristics, we derive an effective activation energy
tuning parameter of 200 $\mu$eV, and an inductive term corresponding to an
effective elemental inductance of 1 nH. Both are many orders of magnitude
larger than expected on the basis of simple capacitance considerations. The
critical voltage is also found to be strongly affected by magnetic field, in
a way that cannot be simply explained by the destruction of coherent quantum
phase slips by magnetic flux quanta. The observations are those expected from
quantum interference between coherent quantum phase slip elements, but with
elements of a mesoscopic rather than nanoscopic size.
  We present a semi-empirical model in which the tuning of the quantum
interference is explained by a fine-tuning of the resistance of the normal
regime of the nanowire, itself tuned by the gate voltage. An inductive term
appears in the effective activation energy of the coherent quantum phase slips,
corresponding to an effective elemental inductance of 1 nH. The resonant behavior
is explained by a critical current of the quantum interference element of 1.3
$\mu$A, and a resistance of interference of 13 k$\Omega$. The model also
explains the observed magnetoresistance, and implies that the coherent quantum
phase slips are not destroyed by magnetic flux quanta, but are instead strongly
suppressed.
  In conclusion, a critical voltage tuning phenomenon has been observed in
NbN nanowires, and explained as a quantum interference between coherent quantum
phase slips, but with a complexity not previously seen in any material.
Simpler explanations (e.g. a traditional quantum point contact) do not fit the
data. The behavior has been successfully modeled as a quantum interference of a
coherent quantum phase slip element with a normal resistance, itself tuned by a
gate voltage.

inferred best-fit solution appears quantitatively unreasonable given the

velocity variability does not persist when analyzed with more modern
high-resolution spectra. While the ultimate cause of the origin of these

viewpoint. In this paper, we propose a framework for novel view video
prediction which learns a dual representation from a set of input video clips

results in an exhaustive way to all possible polarization combinations and
predict full transverse birefringence for scattering of x-ray photons in the

scattering of x-ray photons at even larger scattering angles which are
characteristic for quantum nature of the process.

investigation of the proposed experiments.

involving an anisotropic medium and explain the quantum origin of the
observations made. Finally, we suggest several experimental scenarios to
demonstrate the predictions made in this work.

This latter support clearly underscores the motivation behind this work.

Broadbent and Lord (TQC'20), is an
encryption scheme with the following attractive feature: given a ciphertext, an
adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same
message as the original ciphertext. We revisit this notion and show the
following:
  - Reusability: The constructions proposed by Broadbent and Lord have the
disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. Both of these
constructions can be improved.
  - Tightness: We show tight reductions for unclonable encryption, improving
previous constructions.
  - Composability: We also show a construction of unclonable encryption from
any non-interactive public-key encryption scheme and a minimal (constant number
of interactions is sufficient) protocol for cut-and-choose, extending the
work of Broadbent and Lord.
  - Lower Bounds: We also give a lower bound on the number of interactions
required for any construction of unclonable encryption.
  Our constructions and lower bound use a new, simple, and efficient proof of
knowledge protocol for a computational version of the following problem: "given
a commitment to a number $x$, how to prove ``$x$ is even'' without revealing
more information than what is already committed'. We believe this problem has
potential applications to other cryptographic constructions.
  Our constructions are from the following assumptions: indistinguishability
obfuscation, learning with errors, and passively-secure MPC protocols (which
can be constructed assuming popular assumptions like indistinguishability
obfuscation, NIZK with PPPS, or a threshold implementation of a la FHE). For
the tight reductions, we design new protocols based a novel technique which we
call "look-back protocols". Look-back protocols are generally useful, and can
also be used to improve other constructions of secure multi-party protocols.
  In particular, our constructions for tight reductions are the first to
eliminate the need for complex hash proofs of knowledge.
  We show two instantiations of our composition: (1) A (simple) construction
of a multi-time secure public-domain encryption scheme. (2) A construction of
multi-time secure key-exchange protocol with forward secrecy.
  Finally, we show a construction of a signing scheme from any construction of
unclonable encryption

information-theoretic authentication in additive white Gaussian noise channels,
as long as the adversary is not omniscient. The model considered consists of an
encoder, decoder, and adversary, where the adversary has access to the message,
a non-causal noisy observation of the encoder's transmission, and unlimited
transmission power, while the decoder observes a noisy version of the sum of
the encoder and adversary's outputs. A method to modify a generic existing
channel code to enable authentication is presented. It is shown that this
modification costs an asymptotically negligible amount of the coding rate,
while still enabling authentication as long as the adversary's observation is
not noiseless. Also notable is that this modification is not (asymptotically) a
function of the statistical characterization of the adversary's channel and
furthermore no secret key is required, hence paving the way for a robust
practical implementation. Using these results, the channel-authenticated
capacity is calculated and shown to be equal to the non-adversarial channel
capacity. While this modular scheme is designed for use in the given channel
model, it is applicable to a wide range of settings.

paper shows that if the adversary has a limited transmission power, then a
much simpler modification (than the one for the omniscient adversary) of the
channel code would still enable authentication. The second companion paper

constrained or channeled by magnetic fields that form a surrounding
magnetosphere. The very strong winds of massive stars are understood to be
driven by line-scattering of the star's radiative momentum, while in the Sun
and even lower-mass stars a much weaker mass loss arises from the thermal
expansion of a mechanically heated corona. In exoplanets around such low-mass
stars, the radiative heating and wind interaction can lead to thermal expansion
or mechanical ablation of their atmospheres. Stellar magnetospheres result from
the internal trapping of the wind outflow, while planetary magnetospheres are
typically shaped by the external impact from the star's wind. But in both cases
the stressing can drive magnetic reconnection that results in observable
signatures such as X-ray flares and radio outbursts. This review will aim to

their similarities and distinctions for stars vs. planets.

magnitude of such stresses and the resulting effects can vary greatly. A
comparative study of such systems holds great potential for gaining insight
into general physical processes and their dependence on parameters such as the
Mach number of the flow.

increasingly available, providing opportunities to expand comparative
astrophysics studies with plasma to a larger range of parameters.

neural networks with respect to their inputs. To this end, we provide a simple
technique for computing an upper bound to the Lipschitz constant---for multiple
$p$-norms---of a feed forward neural network composed of commonly used layer
types. Our technique is then used to formulate training a neural network with a
bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimisation problem that can be
solved using projected stochastic gradient methods. Our evaluation study shows
that the performance of the resulting models exceeds that of models trained
with other common regularisers. We also provide evidence that the
hyperparameters are intuitive to tune, demonstrate how the choice of norm for
computing the Lipschitz constant impacts the resulting model, and show that the
performance gains provided by our method are particularly noticeable when only
a small amount of training data is available.

other techniques for enforcing Lipschitz continuity (such as Distillable
Divergences) and answer it with an empirical study showing that our approach
outperforms these techniques. Finally, we give a general argument for why our
approach is guaranteed to converge to a local minimum and provide a constrained
optimisation version of our method that is guaranteed to converge to a global
minimum, while still enforcing the Lipschitz constraint deterministically.

ionization of the hydrogen in the atmosphere by ruling out alternative
explanations such as pickup ions and ions originating from the moon. While the
trailing ionized gas is bound to the planet, the leading edge of the trail
is in free space, making this the leading edge of a planetary ion tail.

the properties of the trail provide a direct measurement of thermal ionization

evidence that wide binary asteroids are more likely to have low masses or

Jurassic-Cretaceous intraplate rift zone between the African and South American
plates during the final breakup of western Gondwana. By quantitatively
accounting for crustal deformation in the Central and West African rift zone,
we indirectly construct the kinematic history of the pre-breakup evolution of
the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins. Our model suggests a causal link
between changes in extension direction and velocity during continental
extension and the generation of marginal structures such as the enigmatic
Pre-salt sag basin and the S\~ao Paulo High. We model an initial E-W directed
extension between South America and Africa (fixed in present-day position) at
very low extensional velocities until Upper Hauterivian times ($\approx$126 Ma)
when rift activity along in the equatorial Atlantic domain started to increase
significantly. During this initial $\approx$17 Myr-long stretching episode the
Pre-salt basin width on the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins is
generated. An intermediate stage between 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian is
characterised by strain localisation, rapid lithospheric weakening in the
equatorial Atlantic domain, resulting in both progressively higher extension
velocities as well as a significant rotation of the extension direction to
NW-SE. Final breakup between South America and Africa occurred between Base
Aptian and Base Albian along a previously underextended region of the lithospheric
plateau located seaward of the present-day Angola-Brazil conjugate margin.
Throughout the rift basin evolution both crustal and the underlying mantle
components of the African plate moved northwestward at velocities of $\approx$
25-30 cm/yr from Base Hauterivian to Base Aptian.
  The kinematic history of the conjugate margins is controlled by a couple of
fundamental factors: (1.) the fixed position of the South American plate in the
present-day global reference frame during all stages of rift basin evolution;
(2.) the progressive acceleration of extensional velocities during two distinct
stretching phases; (3.) the changing extension direction during both stretching
phases; (4.) the differing thermal pre-stretching states of the lithospheric
components of the conjugate margins; and (5.) the differing mantle flow
patterns controlling the rift basin evolution. Our model explains the
generation of several marginal structures in both the Brazilian and the West
African margins, including the Pre-salt basin width

various downstream tasks given limited labeled data. Among various methods,
contrastive learning learns a discriminative representation by constructing
positive and negative pairs. However, it is not trivial to build reasonable
pairs for a segmentation task in an unsupervised way. In this work, we propose
a novel unsupervised pre-training framework for segmentation tasks. Our framework
does not need explicit construction of positive and negative pairs and can
be applied to any organ of interest. Instead of learning a general
discriminative representation, our goal is to learn an attribute-specific
representation, where the attribute is an organ of interest or its category.
To achieve this goal, we propose a novel attribute-guided contrastive learning
framework. Under this framework, a chance-constrained program is designed to
generate semi-sensible hard negative pairs automatically. Extensive experiments
demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in improving segmentation
accuracy when few labeled images are available.
  We also prove the NP-hardness of our problem and design efficient heuristic
algorithms to solve it in polynomial time. Codes are available at:

C (Goal-driven Guidance Generation in Grounded
Communication), for grounded dialogue tasks with a twofold purpose. The
participant of the proposed task engages in a guided dialogue to describe a
three-dimensional scene to a partner who then uses the description to build a
3D model. Our theoretical motivation behind introducing purposeful descriptions
in grounded dialogue is the pursuit of more semantically meaningful
communications, which could lead to better natural language processing (NLP)
models and techniques. To achieve this, we introduce a set of guiding policies
or "roles" with unique goals and policies for generating certain types of
language. At the beginning of each session, a guiding policy is randomly
assigned to the speaker. The speaker's goal is to effectively and efficiently
generate utterances to convey her intended message to the listener. A number of
built-in policies allow the speaker to choose from different levels of
complexity when producing her sentences. As a result, the speaker can easily
adapt to the listener's misbuildings and up the level of conversation if
necessary. We also introduce a set of 3D scenes, referred to as the
University Scenes, as our testbed for the G4C task. With the G4C framework, we
aim to investigate the effectiveness of multi-task learning and learning from
multi-task data in the context of grounded dialogue tasks.
  We introduce the MultiTask Grounded Dialogue Dataset (MTGDD), a collection of
multi-task grounded dialogue datasets, to study the effectiveness of multi-task
learning and learning from multi-task data in the context of grounded dialogue.
With MTGDD, we aim to investigate whether a model that learns to perform
multiple tasks at the same time can outperform a model that is trained on
multi-task data, where different tasks are learned sequentially.
  Our results show that models that learn to perform multiple tasks at the same
time outperform models that are trained on multi-task data. However, the
performance gain due to multi-task learning is limited when there is high task
similarity.
  This paper is an extended version of the report that was presented at IROS
2020. In this extended version, the theoretical motivation behind the proposed
G4C task and the MTGDD is further explained. The listening model used to
evaluate the performance of the MTGDD is also detailed.

process is an open and challenging question in biology. Recent studies classify
the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by analysing the distribution of
a protein's planar projections using topological objects called knotoids. We
approach the analysis of proteins with the same topology by introducing a
topologically inspired statistical method based on fractals. Our method orders
proteins with a given topology in terms of their geometrical complexity while
accounting for differences in sequence length. We find that our method
successfully captures the folding complexity of proteins and yields orders of
magnitudes in geometric folding measures for specific topologies that are
exhibited by natural knotted proteins. Remarkably, certain topologies
exhibited by proteins that fold naturally are also the ones with the simplest
geometry, suggesting that nature optimises the folding process for these
topologies. We further introduce a statistical energy function that successfully
separates the native conformation of a protein from an ensemble of random
structures. Interestingly, both measures show strong correlations between
geometry and native conformation, indicating that geometrical considerations
play an important role in the optimisation of energy for protein folding.
Lastly, by analysing the distribution of planar projections of proteins as
knotoids, and also by introducing a topologically inspired statistical method
based on fractals, our study paves way for incorporating topology and geometry
to biophysical energy functions in order to gain a deeper understanding of the
folding process.

re-use of expensive substrates. However, clear experimental evidence of a
remote mechanism remains elusive. In many cases, due to contaminants at the
transferred graphene/substrate interface, alternative mechanisms such as
pinhole-seeded lateral epitaxy or van der Waals epitaxy can explain the
resulting exfoliatable single-crystalline films. Here, we find that growth of
BaZrO${_3}$ on graphene on water (GOW) is consistent with remote epitaxy. We
show that the growth is mediated by a water layer at the graphene/substrate
interface and careful control of water is crucial. Exfoliated films are
single-crystalline, strain-free, and have near-lattice matched epitaxy
temperatures. Furthermore, we find that pinhole formation on graphene/ Cu
substrates halts growth, while GOW follows remote epitaxy growth mode. Last, we
show that remote epitaxy allows for unique microstructure effects which would
not be possible for pinhole-mediated growth.
  We construct a model that explains the growth by a remote mechanism where
water acts as an epitaxial layer between the graphene and substrate. According
to the model, pinholes as well as contaminants at the graphene/ Cu interfaces
can initiate traditional lateral epitaxy. The model is consistent with all
observed experimental facts. It also explains why pinholes and contaminants
prevent epitaxy on contaminant covered graphene/ water interfaces and why
epitaxy is obtained on clean but not on clean but dry graphene surfaces.
Furthermore, it accounts for the unique microstructure effects which are a
hallmark of remote epitaxy.
  In conclusion, remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene is a highly promising
and versatile technique for synthesis of materials with large lattice
mismatches. Control of the water layer is crucial for the growth and care must
be taken when transferring the graphene/ substrate interface to avoid
contaminants at the interface.

studied for several different models of mixing zones behavior. Depending on the
viscosity function the limiting polymer injection profile is rigorously derived
in case of transverse flow equilibrium assumption, for the Koval model and for
the Todd-Longstaff model. The possible gain of the polymer in comparison to
finite number of slugs is numerically estimated.
  The results show significant benefits of polymer flooding with tapering
compared to discrete polymer slugs, both in terms of residual oil saturation
reduction and the overall cost. The gain strongly depends on the viscosity
model, but it can be as high as a factor of five in terms of residual oil
saturation equivalent to the amount of polymer used.
  A key factor influencing the benefit of polymer tapering is the width of the
mixing zone, which can be of the order of meters. If the mixing zones are
 narrower than 1 m, the benefit of polymer tapering is small.
  The models of mixing zones behavior have an impact on the polymer profile and
the residual saturation at the end of injection. Therefore, the choice of the
model should be supported by core flooding data.
  The estimated values of the residual saturation equivalent to the polymer
used depend on the assumed viscosity function for the mixing zones. The broad
distribution of residual saturation equivalent to the polymer used acquires a
meaningful insight into the variability of oil banking phenomenon during
polymer flooding.
  Overall, the results support the use of polymer in all fields of interest,
irrespective of the structure of the reservoir and the quality of the rock.
Further research is needed to derive the optimal polymer profile(s) and to
investigate the effect of the polymer on the gas invasion and on the
coalescence of the waterflood banks.
  It is also important to measure the graded viscosity in core flooding
experiments and to include this effect in numerical simulations in order to
validate the results obtained in this study and to generally improve the
predictive capabilities of reservoir models.
  Finally, to fully assess the economic benefit of polymer flooding, a cost
model should be developed and used to analyze different scenarios.
  In conclusion polymer flooding with tapering is a very efficient process
leading to significant increase in hydrocarbon recovery and reduction of the
recovery cost. Further research is needed to investigate the optimal polymer
profile and to generally validate the predictions of reservoir models with
core flooding data.

modeling the distribution of portfolio returns across portfolios. We establish
relevant mathematical formulas and propose efficient algorithms, drawing upon
powerful techniques in computational geometry and the literature on splines, to
compute the probability density function, the cumulative distribution function,
and the k-th moment of the probability function. Our algorithmic tools and
implementations efficiently handle portfolios with 10000 assets, and compute
moments of order k with log(k) efficiency in terms of runtime. Our toolboxes
provide an important foundation for the quantitative study and risk management
of portfolios, and could be applied to the study of other topics, such as
clustering and anology measurement.
  In particular, our short-range extrapolation based local kernel method can
efficiently compute the k-th moment, for a given positive integer, say, d, of
portfolio returns that the investor would like to know, provided that the
momentum order k is no greater than d. If the moment order k can be greater
than d, the efficient method is to use the moments from 1 to d, to approximate
the k-th moment. This is because our algorithm can compute moments from 1 to d
with log(k) efficiency in terms of runtime, for portfolios with 10000 assets.
Such efficient approximation is very important in the risk management of
portfolios, as it can significantly reduce the computation time, say from hours
to seconds, for a given portfolio and a given range of moments.
  Our paper is a fundamental contribution to the study of the distribution of
portfolio returns across portfolios. It provides essential mathematical tools,
including the probability density function, the cumulative distribution function
and the moments, and efficient algorithms to compute them, for any given
portfolio and moment order. It proposes robust and important methodologies for
the risk management and performance measurement of portfolios, and may be
applied to the risk management and performance measurement of other systems,
including financial markets, networks and systems.
  Finally, the important connection between the distribution of portfolio
returns and the Holder type risk measures is also discussed.

wearable devices such as
smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on popular activities fail to work on rare activities due to overfitting. In
order to address the challenges, we propose a novel framework called FedHealth
which combines federated transfer learning and data aggregation. Specifically,
we design a framework to aggregate deep models trained on non-private user
data for activities at large, and fine-tune the aggregated models for rare
activities through federated transfer learning. We evaluate our approach on two
popular wearable datasets. Experimental results show that our approach could
produce accurate prediction results for rare activities with minimal
fine-tuning data. It also outperforms traditional transfer learning methods
considering the benefits of federated learning.

is crucial for yield optimization and process stability. Yet, in situ
temperature measurements with spatial and temporal resolution are still
challenging. In this work, we perform temperature measurements in a cylindrical
fixed bed reactor by combining the capabilities of real-time magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) with the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF)
shift of water. Three-dimensional (3D) temperature maps are acquired while
heating the bed from room temperature to 60~$^{\circ}$C using hot air. The
obtained results show a clear temperature gradient along the axial and radial
dimensions and agree with optical temperature probe measurements with an
average error of $\pm$ 1.5~$^{\circ}$C. We believe that MR imaging has a great
potential to provide spatiotemporally resolved temperature distributions in
reacting fixed beds, and we look forward to exploiting this technique to
investigate gas--solid mass transfer and reaction hotspots in the bed.
  From a methodological standpoint, we believe that exploiting the PRF shift of
a liquid phase, such as water, to this end is preferable over using the
thermal expansion of the water proton chemical shift, as the latter is orders of
magnitude smaller and requires much more sophisticated spectral processing to
discern. Furthermore, we find that any water present in the bed, be it from
experiments with moist gas or from thermal gravity-driven water vapor
condensation, is advantageous for temperature mapping, as it provides a
concentrated source of MR signal for the purposes of temperature mapping. In
addition, we observe that the MR signal from the bed material (in this case,
silica) is quite strong and does not shift with temperature, which makes it
uitable for reference signal generation. Finally, we find that by using a
positive-gradient spin warp (PGSW) encoding scheme the axial temperature
gradients are readily discernible from the MR images without having to
reconstruct 3D temperature maps from raw MR data.

preconditioners for cardiac mechanics on both structured and unstructured
finite element meshes. The mechanical behavior of myocardium can be described
by the equations of three-dimensional finite elasticity, which are discretized
by finite elements in space and yield the solution of a large scale nonlinear
algebraic system. This problem is solved by a Newton-Krylov method, where the
solution of the Jacobian linear system is accelerated by BDDC/AMG
preconditioners. We thoroughly explore the main parameters of the BDDC
preconditioner in order to make the comparison fair. We focus on: the
performance of different direct solvers for the local and coarse problems of
the BDDC algorithm; the impact of the different choices of BDDC primal degrees
of freedom; and the influence of the fine grid problem size. We report the
results obtained from a series of numerical experiments designed specifically
for this work, which include both synthetic (e.g. the heart of a rabbit) and
real (the human heart in a simplified geometry) tests.
  We show that, for unstructured meshes, the BDDC preconditioner can be even
faster than the AMG preconditioner for the scalar elasticity problem (used as
a proxy for the cardiac one). Furthermore, for a problem of size $134,651$ on
unstructured tetrahedral finite elements, the BDDC preconditioner can solve a
Jacobian linear system in less than $10$ seconds when used in a
Newton-Krylov algorithm for the solution of the full cardiac problem (including
electro-mechanical activation, mass transport and energy balance equations).
In this case, it achieves an iterative convergence rate larger than $10$ in
all iterations and it solves the linear system in an average time per iteration
of $0.12$ seconds on $24$ cores. Finally, for a problem large enough to be
unpractical for the use of either a direct or an iterative solver ($282,821$

people to change their behaviours (e.g., to buy products online). Deep neural
networks have made tremendous progress in generating high-quality videos;
however, training such networks to generate video sequences that persuasively
affect people's emotions and behaviours (i.e., affective trajectories)
remains challenging. One reason is that affective trajectories are often
uncontrollable, making it difficult to collect large quantities of data with
high-quality affective responses. To address this problem, we propose a novel
framework, CoGAN, for training generative adversarial networks (GANs) to
produce affective trajectories, which lead human viewers to naturally exhibit
certain emotional responses (e.g., happiness, sadness) while watching the
generated video. In particular, our model consists of two sub-GANs: a low-level
video generator that produces video frames and a high-level affect emulator
that generates affect trajectories as auxiliary inputs to the video generator
to guide the generated video towards the target affective trajectories.
Further, to ensure the generated video is temporally coherent and smooth,
CoGAN comprises a temporal adaption module. Finally, a critic network evaluates
the affective affectiveness of the generated video from human perspectives.
Extensive experiments show that CoGAN produces videos that receive higher
emotional ratings from viewers as well as lower red flags (i.e., abnormal
behaviors) in terms of watching habits compared to baselines.

  Process discovery is the technique to reconstruct a process from its event
data. Such technique is essential for organizations to understand their
business processes, to improve their processes, and to recharge their
infrastructures. However, the reconstructed processes by existing approaches
often contain noise and impurity, which can lead to wrong process
interpretations or optimization. In order to reduce such unwanted features, we
propose a filtering technique based on the structural properties of the
generated process models to remove unnecessary events and to improve the
quality of the reconstructed processes. We applied our approach on several
event data sets collected from the real-world and common process datasets.

a reentrant transition. We further propose that this phenomenon can be
qualitatively captured by a dimerized tight-binding model with long-range

made of cylinders with a polaron-like arrangement exhibit a reentrant
delocalization transition. We explain this phenomenon to be a result of a
balance between diagonal (on-site) and long-range coupling effects. Indeed, if
the latter exceeds a certain threshold, the states become localized at the
center of the unit cell, but if the on-site coupling is strong enough, the
states are localized at the unit ends and become delocalized in the between-units
regions.

width at half maximum (FWHM) of the decay length profile of the intensity
along the quasicrystal, which increases with increasing modulation strength in
the middle of the band gap. Numerical simulation using a dimerized model
clearly explains such behavior. The proposed dimerized model is the simplest
possible to describe the localization of waves in quasicrystals and readily
available numerical tools can be used to explore the full spectral properties
of the system.

localized-delocalized reentrant transition in one-dimensional photonic
quasicrystals and provides a simple model to numerically investigate such
phenomena in general.

paper, a two-trophic ecosystem comprising of two species of predators,
competing for their common prey, with explicit interference competition is
considered. With proper rescaling, the model is portrayed as a singularly
perturbed system with fast prey dynamics and slow dynamics of the predators. In
a parameter regime near singular Hopf bifurcation, chaotic mixed-mode
oscillations (MMOs), featuring concatenation of small and large amplitude
oscillations are observed as long-lasting transients before the system
approaches its asymptotic state. To analyze the dynamical role of interference
competition, we provide a switch-off scenario, where the interference term is
temporarily turned off, and show that the presence of interference competition
is necessary to generate complex dynamics such as MMOs in this system. A
novel technique to provide a qualitative estimate of the duration of
transient chaos is provided. Early indication of sudden regime shift in this
system is provided by abrupt decrease in the root-mean-square (RMS) gap
distance indicating sudden shift from transient chaos to asymptotic state.
RMS gap distance of the systems producing MMOs is found to possess long memory
of about 100 natural time units. Such sudden shifts in such complex systems
can be an early indicator of sudden population collapse.

appropriate management strategies, provided the underlying competition model

multi-species ecosystems can present complex dynamical indicators of sudden
regime shifts, both at the population level as well as at the level of individual
animals, thus having wide applicability to study sudden regime shifts in
ecosystems.

leading to sudden regime shifts in ecological systems. The results presented
here can be applied to a variety of systems with competing species to study
early indicators of sudden regime shifts.

should explicitly consider the dynamical effects of competition on population
dynamics.

counter an epidemic phenomenon observed in cache coherence protocols --
instructions induced by memory accesses reappear after program restarts.

in cache coherence design, the technique employed is general and can be
applied, with some modifications, to other similar scenarios. The paper presents
a set of techniques -- our core contribution -- to which our model is fundamentally
attached. The model itself is a set of rules that, with some minor complexity,
can be used to check if a cache coherence protocol preserves program behaviors
between program executions. This is the first such model for cache coherence
protocols proposed so far. It is the foundation of our work and has important
implications for the area, potentially leading to a better understanding of the
relationship between cache coherence protocols and programs that use them.
Further, our contribution highlights the importance of clear program behaviors
specifications for programs to be run with a particular protocol and how such
specifications can be automatically generated. Additionally, our study shows the
importance of program behaviors to the evaluation of cache coherence protocols.
It highlights that only considering execution time as the metric to evaluate
cache coherence protocols can lead to unreasonable results.

Microbenchmark and the whole NAS parallel benchmarks from PARSEC. Our results
show that a small set of instructions can cause significant program behaviors
between program restarts, indicating the importance of considering such
behaviors in program-to-protocol mappings. Moreover, our study demonstrates how
cache coherence protocols can lead to an explosion of program behaviors if
carefully designed. Such observation underlines the need for specifying and
preserving program behaviors in cache coherence protocols.

3k-4 theorem states that if A and B are subsets
of the integers of size k with small sumset (of size close to 2k) then they are
very close to arithmetic progressions. Our aim in this paper is to strengthen
this by allowing only a bounded number of possible sums that are missed by A
and B. We also allow for some of the elements of A and B to be repeated, while
still bounding the number of possible different elements that A and B can
contain. Finally, we allow for the possibility that A and B are not quite
subsets, but rather are multsets (i.e.\ they can contain the same element
repeatedly).
  In doing so, we obtain a new quantification of the measure of the sets A and
B for which the above conclusion holds. This, in turn, leads to new results in
graph theory (concerning the monochromatic sum of squares problem) and also
strengthens the basis of many other applications of 3k-4, in particular by
enabling us to apply it to classes of sets which were previously outside its
scope.
  In particular, we prove a new version of the variable strength 3k-4 theorem
in which not only the number of elements but also the number of pairs of
elements and, in some cases, the number of triples of elements is bounded. We
also use this to solve a problem raised by Shalom and Weiss in geometric
group theory.
  Finally, we introduce a new quantification of the strength of 3k-4 type
theorems, capturing the trade-off between the range of application and the
strength of the conclusion. We then apply this to compare the strength of various
variations of 3k-4.

features with predictive information of
patients that develop severe symptoms of COVID-19. If true, this hypothesis may
have practical value in allocating resources to particular patients while using
a relatively inexpensive imaging technique. The difficulty of testing such a
hypothesis comes from the need for large sets of labelled data, which need to
be well-annotated and should contemplate the post-imaging severity outcome.
This paper presents an original methodology for extracting semantic features
that correlate to severity from a data set with patient ICU admission labels
through interpretable models. The methodology employs a neural network trained
to recognise lung pathologies to extract the semantic features, which are then
analysed with low-complexity models to limit overfitting while increasing
interpretability. This analysis points out that only a few features explain
most of the variance between patients that developed severe symptoms. When
applied to an unrelated larger data set with pathology-related clinical notes,
the method has shown to be capable of selecting images for the learned
features, which could translate some information about their common locations
in the lung. Besides attesting separability on patients that eventually develop
severe symptoms, the proposed methods produce interpretable results when compared
to other deep learning architectures.
  From the results, four semantic features, which can be viewed as descriptions
of common patterns of lung pathology, were found to be strongly related to the
development of severe symptoms (p < 0.0009). Three out of such features were
capable of completely separate patients that developed severe symptoms from the
rest of the patients (sensitivity = specificity = 100\%). When applied to an
unrelated larger data set with clinical notes, the features were capable of
selecting images that contain most common descriptions related to the proposed
pathology patterns. Stronger separation was found when compared to other deep
learning architectures, which could point out overfitting.

Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). We observe that during training, the
relationship proposal distribution is highly imbalanced: most of the negative
relationship proposals are easy to identify, e.g., the inaccurate object

proposals. This paper presents Spatially-Aware Balanced negative pRoposal

model to classify all 128,000+ negative proposals during training. BNPS is
completely differentiable and has little influence on training speed and

recognition in the dark.
In this work, we present our results on the ARID dataset. Most previous works
only evaluate performance on large, well illuminated datasets like Kinetics and
HMDB51. We demonstrate that our work is able to achieve a very low error rate
while being trained on a much smaller dataset of dark videos. We also explore a
variety of training and inference strategies including domain transfer
methodologies and also propose a simple but useful frame selection strategy.
Our empirical results demonstrate that we beat previously published baseline
models by 11%.
  We also observe that as the darkness of the test videos increase, models
trained with our proposed framework degenerate less than models trained with
other domain transfer techniques.
  Finally, we also observe that our frame selection strategy improves
performance on all light conditions by up to 8% suggesting that our basic
approach is not sophisticated enough and there is still room for further
improvement.

Addressable Parallel Processor using a FPGA. While Content addressable memories

parallel write and other features of a CAPP.

generator. This requires making the connection between the symbolic
representation of the code, typically used by a static program analyzer, and
the string representation that a neural model consumes and produces. We
identifify two challenges: (1) most neural code generation methods produce
symbolically-analyzed, yet abstract syntax tree representations as output;
(2) there is a lack of a systematic approach to map the results of a static
program analyzer onto neural input/output. For the second challenge, we
propose a general framework that uses feature functions to address this
mapping. Our method, QSCode, achieves better performance on longer code
generations, while remaining general to code in languages supported by a
static program analyzer.

detecting anomalous data
streams such as network intrusions, temperature fluctuations in a process
plant, and false positives in image recognition systems among others. Anomaly
detection starts by modeling normal behavior and then identifies anomalies as
a departure from this model. Although anomaly detection models work well
initially, they deteriorate over time, accumulating false positives and
withdrawing from normal data as well. The main challenge in anomaly detection
is to reduce the number of false positives, which means improving the ability
of the model to distinguish normal data from anomalous data. A number of
research work use generative models such as VAE to model normal behavior and
detect anomalies. The main shortcoming of these models is that they require
large amounts of labeled data, both normal and anomalous, and also a lot of
time to train. Furthermore, they require to be trained from scratch for every
different kind of anomaly detection problem. To address these issues, we
propose a new framework based on a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) that allows
to model normal behavior of streams in an unsupervised way and our framework
has a new component called StreamAnomalyDetector which allows to detect
anomalies based on the normal behavior model. StreamAnomalyDetector is a
Windows Anomaly Detector, it runs in constant time independent of the stream
size and it is scalable to handle high volume streams. It also allows user
to specify level of anomalies to return per unit of time and only returns the
most anomalous data based on a novel uncertainty based scoring function.
StreamAnomalyDetector has been tested on a number of anomaly detection
domains. The experimental results show that it returns high quality anomalous
data and it outperforms the state of the art methods.
  This paper presents a new framework for modeling normal behavior in data
streams using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and a new component called

based models show good performance on Euclidean data spaces yet struggle on

hypergraph neural network that uses hyperedges to model higher-order interactions

their effect on the output. It uses hyperedge attention to selectively aggregate
information from all possible combinations of hyperedges. It uses residual
learning to train our model that minimizes the categorical hinge loss. HGCN

Instagram meme dataset and the WeAreAllAnonymous dataset.

) is a novel minimally invasive
treatment that is used to ablate intracranial structures to treat mesial
temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Region of interest (ROI) segmentation before and
after LITT would enable automated lesion quantification to objectively assess
treatment efficacy. Deep learning techniques, such as convolutional neural
networks (CNNs) are state-of-the-art solutions for ROI segmentation, but
require large amounts of annotated data during the training. However,
collecting large datasets from emerging treatments such as LITT is impractical.
In this paper, we propose a progressive brain lesion synthesis framework
(PAVAE) to expand both the quantity and diversity of the training dataset.
Concretely, our framework consists of two sequential networks: a mask synthesis
network and a mask-guided lesion synthesis network. To better employ extrinsic
information to provide additional supervision during network training, we
design a condition embedding block (CEB) and a mask embedding block (MEB) to
encode inherent conditions of masks to the feature space. Finally, a
segmentation network is trained using raw and synthetic lesion images to
evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Experimental results show
that our method can achieve realistic synthetic results and boost the
performance of down-stream segmentation tasks above traditional data
augmentation techniques.
  We utilize an open-source atlas-based MTLE dataset (i.e., KAIST-MTLE) to
evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in the context of lesion
segmentation. Our method achieves the highest Dice score of 0.8733 compared to
other state-of-the-art GAN architectures. Meanwhile, our framework also
demonstrates outstanding performance when tested with raw lesion images.
Besides, experimental results show that our framework can boost the performance
of down-stream segmentation tasks above traditional data augmentation techniques.
Therefore, our proposed framework is a viable solution for the lesion
segmentation of the MTLE dataset.

whether a factor should be encoded linearly or orthogonally. We propose a new
efficient algorithm for optimizing the criterion in such case and show its
correct selection properties in a sparse scenario. The most important advantage

ophysical computational model of brain
regions relevant to Parkinson's Disease based on local field potential data
collected from the brain of marmoset monkeys. Parkinson's disease is a
neurodegenerative disorder, linked to the death of dopaminergic neurons at the
substantia nigra pars compacta, which affects the normal dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain. Although there are
multiple mechanisms underlying the disease, a complete description of those
mechanisms and molecular pathogenesis are still missing, and there is still no
cure. To address this gap, computational models that resemble neurobiological
aspects found in animal models have been proposed. In our model, we performed a
data-driven approach in which a set of biologically constrained parameters is
optimised using differential evolution. Evolved models successfully recapitulate
several aspects of the non-disease and disease states of the neurophysiological
data. As importantly, the learned mechanisms in the models are based on
biological processes found in the living primate brain. In addition, we show
how our model can be used to compute back the neurotransmitter release related
to the dynamics observed in the local field potential data. This work shows an
example of a computational model that could be used to study Parkinson's
Disease mechanisms as well as evaluate future treatments, and it illustrates
how machine learning can be used to perform biologically inspired optimisation
of neurobiological parameters.

multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the turbulent convective regime.

difficulty would be in limiting spurious growth of the fluctuations in the
direction of the mean wind, as this can dominate the mean flow as much as the

dynamical system. This bound is fast enough to have a significant effect, and
results in a more cellular (and therefore computationally efficient) flow than
if no such bound were included. Results are presented from a series of
single-column tests, showing that the variance of the fluctuations is maintained
at a constant multiple of the square of the mean flow, and that this multiple
is dependent only on the strength of the sub-filter variability, not on the
strength of the mean flow as it would be in a simple diffusion-based bound.
Further, in a prototypical three-dimensional model, the bound has the effect of
preventing excessive growth and maintenance of large horizontal variances in a
dry convective atmosphere.

separation of scales between the mean flow and the fluctuations, may be able to
remove the need for such bounds altogether.

through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of

with a small number of trials. Further, the results indicate that the impact

pressure affect yield and profit.

management and evaluate whether the findings can be generalized to other
industries.

regions of constant activity, where otherwise the potential would be minimum.

corresponds to a constant velocity of the dimer in the activity gradient.

reinforcement learning by exploiting the expert demonstrations. However, in
many real scenarios, obtaining expert demonstrations could be extremely
expensive or even impossible. To overcome this challenge, in this paper, we
propose a novel learning framework called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL) to
exploit the past good experiences of the agents themselves without expert
demonstration. Specifically, we train two different agents via letting each of
them alternately explore the environment and exploit the peer agent's
experience. While the experiences could be of poor quality due to random
exploration, we devise a novel adversarial estimation network to improve the
utility of the experiences by discriminating between good and bad ones. The
co-imitation learning framework is able to produce high-performance policies
with a small number of interactions to the environment. Experimental results
demonstrate that our approach surpasses the state-of-the-art by an order of
magnitude in terms of the sample complexity.
  We also study the theoretical properties of the proposed co-updating
strategy. Specifically, we prove that our algorithm is guaranteed to produce
a joint policy that is as good as the best policy among the two. However, the
guarantee comes at the cost of quadratic increase of policy evaluations. To
reduce the number of policy evaluations, a practical variant of the co-updating
is also provided.

produced by RL for NMT are mostly due to promoting tokens that have already
received a fairly high probability in pre-training. We hypothesize that the
large action space is a main obstacle to RL's effectiveness in MT, and conduct
two sets of experiments that lend support to our hypothesis. First, we find
that reducing the size of the vocabulary improves RL's effectiveness. Second,
we find that effectively reducing the dimension of the action space without
changing the vocabulary also yields notable improvement as evaluated by BLEU,
semantic similarity, and human evaluation. Indeed, by initializing the
network's final fully connected layer (that maps the network's internal
dimension to the vocabulary dimension), with a layer that generalizes over
similar actions, we obtain a substantial improvement in RL performance: 1.5
BLEU points on average.
  Our results demonstrate the power of analyzing RL for NMT from a perspective
of the action space, and how reducing the vocabulary size and the dimension of
the action space can lead to better performance.

behavior, general affect towards opposing partisans and their parties, and
contents posted and consumed online. Research over the years has focused on the
role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users
alongside careful measurements of the time spent browsing various news sources.
We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of users' search behavior in polarization. By scrutinizing search
queries issued by users before their visits to news sites, we find a large
presence of direct searches for news topics, but surprisingly little evidence
of search biases that could lead to further polarization. Most importantly,
search behavior does not appear to play an important role in driving polarization
of Web browsing habits. Instead, we find strong evidence of partisan biases in
how search queries related to current events are partitioned across different
news sources, hinting at the role of search as a tool for information retrieval
rather than navigation across different domains.
  Overall, our work offers comprehensive evidence of and novel insights into
the factors behind Web polarization.
  We make our data and analyses publicly available.
  Future research along the lines developed in this work has the potential of
delving into the complex relationship between polarization and the increasingly
prevailing use of private browsing modes among the public.
  It can also further quantify the effect of polarization on the economic
success of different news domains, as well as investigate how different
regulatory interventions could affect news consumption and, in turn, polarization.
Finally, future research can further develop and apply new methods for
reconstructing browsing behavior from popular search queries, as we demonstrate
in Section 4.
  As search engines continue to play an increasingly prominent role in
shaping people's online experiences \cite{B\"ohling2020}, studying how they
interact with polarization is an important and timely task that we leave for
future work.

that evaluates each finite word over A_p={0,1,...,p-1} to some rational number.
We let N_p/q denote the image of this evaluation function. In particular, N_p/q

focuses on the set of words that are evaluated to nonnegative integers; it is a
rather chaotic language which is not context-free. On the contrary, we study
here the subsets of (N_p/q)^d that are p/q-recognisable, i.e. realised by
finite automata over (A_p)^d. First, we give a characterisation of these sets
as those definable in a first-order logic, similar to the one given by the
B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer bases numeration systems. Second, we show
that the natural order relation and the modulo-q operator are not
p/q-recognisable.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often lead to
misclassification of related patterns. In medical imaging, this limitation can
result in correct classifications of individual structures to be prevented
across related anatomies. For instance, brain tumors made of glioma and
meningioma tissues may be classified uniformly, irrespective of their
morphological appearances. Recently, Dual-Path Network (DPN) has successfully
fused both textures and edges by introducing an edge understanding path in CNNs.
However, its ability to distinguish across related anatomies, an important
requirement in medical imaging, is yet to be explored. In this work, we propose
an extension of Dual-Path Network as a pre-trained module for arbitrary sets of
anatomies. We hypothesize that a customized combination of multiple DPNs, each
trained for a set of related anatomies, may learn to distinguish between
anatomies while retaining the generalization ability for new patterns.
Specifically, we minimize negative classifications among anatomies within a
domain and maximize generalization performance across domains. We evaluate our
method on three publicly available brain segmentation datasets, showing
improvements over state-of-the-art methods. We also show our method achieves
higher performance on new brain structures than a model trained on existing
data alone.

data via hindsight summarization to minimize attended prediction error, similar
to an online prompt engineering problem. This is made feasible by the use of a

learning problem with online prompt engineering, and is made possible by the
pretraining of the network and the use of a receptive field (resampling).
Simulations show that this approach is effective for few-shot continual learning
and agrees with human memory mechanisms for learning from experience.
Furthermore, it shows that resampling (by a memory policy) can be more
effective than relabeling (by hindsight graph) alone. It also shows how a
receptive field (a form of attention) can improve performance by filtering
noise. It also shows that a contrastive value policy can be reduced to a
contrastive policy via a radial decay of excellence (attained goals). Most

Biases in the dataset can be learned by the model and degrade the
generalizability of the applications. There are studies on debiased models.
However, scientists and practitioners are difficult to identify implicit biases
in the datasets, which causes lack of reliable unbias test datasets to valid
models. To tackle this issue, we first define the data intrinsic bias
attribute, and then propose a novel bias identification framework for medical
image datasets. The framework contains two major components, KlotskiNet and
Bias Identification using Deep Equalization Technique (BIDET). KlotskiNet is a
small-sized contrastive learning based patch level classifier to identify
implicit biases by exploiting dissimilarities between training with random
label and testing samples. BIDET is used to collect unbiased test datasets by
fine-tuning a model on the biased dataset and calculating the improvement on
performance. We utilize the biased and unbiased test datasets to validate the
effectiveness of the proposed framework on two commonly used anatomical
segmentation datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework is
useful for assessing the presence of implicit biases in medical image
datasets.

social graphs have revealed their higher-order architecture, which can be
described by aggregates of simplexes (triangles, tetrahedrons, and higher
cliques). Current research aims at quantifying these hidden geometries to
understand their function and dynamics. Most of these efforts focus on
(geo)distances between nodes and links in networks, while simplex membership
itself has been largely overlooked. We introduce Hyperedges, a module for
calculating simplexes in undirected and directed networks. It provides an
intuitive interface to extract triangles and higher-order hyperedges as well as
their properties such as the number of hyperedges, nodes with the most
outliers, and nodes with the highest hyperedge load. Calculations can be
performed quickly for medium-sized networks but also efficiently for large
networks using approximations or out-of-core computation. With the United
States of America air travel network and the brain network of the fruit fly
Drosophila melanogaster as examples, we show how Hyperedges can help in
investigating network geometry and its relation to network function and
structure. Hyperedges is available under the 3-Clause BSD License at

presentation focuses on the eigenvalue problems rather than the wavelet

  From the theoretical point of view acoustic emission (AE) or crackling noise
is the superposition of sudden, short-lived spikes resulting from sudden
failures of local stress concentrators in a system undergoing dynamic failure.
Such failures occur as a result of fast, nonlinear dynamics governed by a
potential energy landscape with multiple local minima. The exact form of the
potential is unknown for any real system. Moreover, being of complex nature, a
combined experimental and theoretical investigation on the topic is scarce. In
view of such complexities and constraints, understanding AE from strongly
nonlinear point contact system, such as that of a peel-ing tape, may provide
insights into the problem.

exhibits an interesting property of having maximum correlation dimension at a
specific velocity. This peculiar observation of dynamical stabilization of a
chaotic system is explained on basis of a simplified model that takes into
account both the stick-slip as well as the rubber like behaviour of the tape.

acoustic emission in the context of a peel-ing tape.

manufacturing, communication networks, biology and medicine, defense and
national security, and a host of other sectors over the past decades. However,
accurately and efficiently modeling CPA- and NLO-based laser systems is

methods. Here, we present a unifying software framework that integrates
state-of-the-art CPA and NLO modeling capabilities into a single, modular,

accuracy, we model 10 different reference systems, including both
experimental and theoretical test cases, and show that it predicts their
performance with high precision. With LIMELight, we aim to provide a reliable,

reverse engineering, and optimization of existing as well as next-generation

technological breakthroughs and fundamental scientific discoveries.

development and maintenance, we have structured LIMELight into modular
sub-routines, following a object-oriented programming style, which makes it
relatively easy to modify or replace any component without affecting the

between counter-propagating modes under the contacts placed in certain
locations. Thus, neutral modes carry information that can be used to nonlocally
reconstruct a dc charge current. Our protocol can be used to detect any neutral
mode that counterpropagates with respect to all charge modes. Our protocol
applies not only to the edge modes of a quantum Hall system, but also to
systems that have neutral modes of non-quantum Hall origin. We conclude with a
possible experimental realization of this phenomenon.

Quantum Hall systems possess charge modes that are both gapped and chiral.
Here we consider systems with more than one type of mode, where some of the
modes are charge modes and others are neutral (i.e. do not carry electric
current, although they may carry heat current). We establish that when there
are modes that are charge modes in one direction but neutral in the perpendicular
direction, then they cannot all be confining. Such modes are an example of
non-orientable modes of quantum Hall systems. We establish general criteria for
the existence of such modes. Furthermore, we establish that, under certain
conditions, they cannot exist at all fillings where there is an insulator in a
different class.

approach based on the bulk polarization density. Another way is the surface
approach based on the surface charge layer. We show that these two views are
equivalent, and there is no need for an ad-hoc surface Hamiltonian as recently

of the light-matter interaction, which can be useful in the context of
photoinduced dynamics.
  From a mathematical point of view, the different views and representations of
the light-matter interaction can be understood by considering the rank of the
momentum operator in the TB scheme. For the standard cell-size approach the
rank is 3, which implies that the product of two momentum operators is
proportional to the identity operator. For the surface approaches the rank is
2, which implies that the product of two momentum operators is proportional to
the spatial overlap of two states. Finally, for the current-matrix element
representation the rank of the momentum operator depends on its orientation;
in particular, it is 1 for the x, y, and z components.

sodium chloride (NaCl) using different views and representations of the
light-matter interaction. We find that photoconductivity and photoabsorption
are well described by all views and representations considered.

interaction that can be used for any material and any orientation of the
electric field.

Neural Networks (CNN) and Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been successfully used for process-mining tasks.
They have achieved better performance for different predictive tasks than
traditional approaches. We extend the existing body of research by testing four
different variants of Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and a fully connected
Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) with dropout for the tasks of predicting the
nature and timestamp of the next process activity. In contrast to existing
studies, our dataset includes both sequence and graph information about the
processes. The experimental results show that the performance of GNNs is high
and very competitive with existing deep-learning approaches, who use also other
types of data but do not exploit the complex structure contained in our
dataset.
  We argue that GNNs are capable of learning very complex predictive tasks
without hand-engineered design choices (features). However, in contrast to
traditional neural approaches, their performance is limited by the scope of the
graph they are trained upon. Both synthetic and real-world experiments indicate
that higher predictive performance can be achieved when more relevant
information about the processes is available.
  We argue that both existing studies and our work have some limitations,
namely that they are mostly evaluated on small datasets and they do not
introduce a standardized framework for evaluating deep-learning approaches on
processes. Future studies should consider more advanced evaluation settings
such as controlled multi-task scenarios and single-task settings with
comparable baseline approaches.

studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, after which most of the methods have better performance than the
best-performing method before normalization. This work opens up the possibility
to critically assess and compare the performance of new methods as more are
proposed.
  From a statistical physics perspective, the critical question is not whether
normalized scores work, but how they work, what they imply, and whether they
generalize to other systems. Further, the connection between the underlying
network structure (caused by the underlying system of interactions) and
normalized scores is still lacking. Ideally, the connection would allow us to
infer parameters of a model describing the underlying system from polarization
alone. We outline how to study this connection in generically structured
social networks formed by a spatial latent position model. We hope that our
work will encourage a statistical and principled study of complex systems and
will provide essential tools to assess whether statistical models of
dynamical systems really work.

effect in magnetic materials with
vanishing magnetization has renewed interest in understanding and engineering
this phenomenon. Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites are one of emerging material
classes that exhibit a variety of interesting properties owing to a complex
electronic band structure and magnetic ordering. Reports on the anomalous
Nernst effect and its magnitude in this class of materials are, however, very
limited. This scarcity may be partly due to the experimental difficulty of
reliably quantifying the anomalous Nernst coefficient. Here, we report
experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite
Mn$_3$NiN thin films. Measurement of both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects
using the same sample and measurement geometry makes it possible to directly
compare these two effects and quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and
conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. We carefully evaluate the spatial distribution of
the thermal gradient in the sample and use finite element modeling to
corroborate our experimental results.
  From the measured anomalous Nernst coefficient, we deduce the
spin-orbit-coupled scattering lifetime of electrons in Mn$_3$NiN. The
anomalous Nernst conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN is found to be much larger than
that in previously reported materials, indicating that the anomalous Nernst
conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN originats from a combination of a large anomalous
Nernst coefficient and a large electrical conductivity.
  Finally, we compare the magnitude of the anomalous Nernst conductance in
Mn$_3$NiN to other materials in the limit of zero magnetic field and find that
Mn$_3$NiN has one of the largest values, even better than some of the rare
earth ferromagnets that exhibit a large spontaneous magnetization.
  In conclusion, the anomalous Nernst conductance in Mn$_3$NiN is superior to
that in most previously reported materials, making it one of the most promising
materials for anomalous Nernst effect applications.

professional work, but it lacked the vision that was necessary to lead an
institute of that size and quality to the top in a field that was increasingly
demanding for innovation and large resources. Under his directorate the
institution lost some of its leading positions in research and its influence
on the development of astronomy in general. After van Rhijn it developed
further under other directors into what it is now.

obtaining the funds needed from the government and privately to make the
catalogue really useful for quantitative research. He was unfortunate in
finding himself in between two scientific giants, and his own scientific
status was intermediate between them both in terms of quality of research and
influence on the development of astronomy.

staff employed at the institute and even managed to persuade the Netherlands
Government to continue to fund the institute at its pre-depression level. In
general van Rhijn showed himself during his directorate as a professional
astronomer of high moral standards who never deviated from his path towards
making Kapteyn's ideas a reality and never attempted to advance himself by

people in society, asking ourselves whether individual intelligence is
necessary in order to collective wisdom to emerge and, most importantly, what
sort of individual intelligence is conducive of greater collective wisdom. We

psychology, economics and physics, casting them in terms of changing structure
of the system's Lyapunov function. Finally, we apply these insights to the sort
and degrees of intelligence of preys and predators in the Lotka-Volterra model,
explaining why certain individual understandings lead to co-existence of the
two species whereas other usages of their individual intelligence cause global
extinction.
  We show that non-transitive thinking, akin to ambiguity or uncertainly, is
necessary for the emergence of collective wisdom whether in a model of
interaction based on cooperation in the presence of defection or in one based
on competition itself. Collective wisdom does not emerge when interactions are
either entirely cooperative or entirely competitive. If it does emerge, as in
the case of Lotka-Volterra's predators and preys, certain sorts of individual
intelligence enhance, rather than diminish, collective wisdom.
  Our results suggest that endowing agents with a degree of ambiguity, that is,
with the ability to have uncertain perceptions of their environment may be a
necessary step towards the development of models of collective wisdom. Such
sort of individual intelligence cannot be guaranteed but it appears to be a
necessary step towards the emergence of collective wisdom.
  If this needed degree of uncertainty is not inherent in the rules of
interaction of the agents, as in the case of cooperation in the presence of
defection, it must be imposed externally. Imposition of uncertainty amounts to
adding randomness to the system, which explains why many models of collective
wisdom built with stochastic rules do indeed exhibit wisdom. The question

the COVID pandemic impacts
students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had a higher percentage of engaged modules during regular
semesters. There was no significant change in submission behavior for women and
non-first-generation students. Overall, the impact of remote learning was more
pronounced for more populous demographic groups, with an increase in early
submission for the majority group and no change in on-time submission for the
minority groups.

multidimensional space, but by mapping the interval [0, inf) to that region, it

impractically in size as the number of entities increases. We ask, can we
structure these growth patterns following established laws in nature and
biology? Can we anticipate future node additions following prescribed
rules? Most existing graph generation methods cannot provide such answers,

we first identify common relational data distributions in the real world and
analyze their corresponding node addition patterns. Based on the analysis, we
propose a new parameterized graph generation model that anticipates future
node additions following prescribed rules. To demonstrate the usefulness of
our approach, we show that it improves the performance of existing graph
completion and recommendation methods on datasets with anticipated node
growth.

introduce in this paper. We study how different generators produce similar but
distinct topological profiles by introducing new parameters to control the
production of certain topological features in the most flexible generators.

distinct latent structural features, confirming that different generators
produce different topological profiles. Moreover, most of the topological
features of the generated networks follow similar distributions as the
extremes of the range of the number of reticulations are reached first. We
emphasize that comparing different generators is a comparison between parameter
settings, where the choice of range of the number of reticulations is most
important. Finally, we propose a new parameter, the {\em topological
distance}, to quantify the structural dissimilarity between the topological
profiles of two generators.
