network theory, this work studies the extremal gain of optimal power control
over binary (on/off) power control, especially in large interference networks,
in search of new theoretical insights. While numerical studies have already
established that in most practical settings binary power control is close to
optimal, the extremal analysis shows not only the existence of a positive
gap between the extremal gain of optimal and binary power control for large
network size, but also bounds the gap from below. Thus extremal analysis of
power control yields a non-trivial result, showing the necessity of considering
over a discrete state space to study a continuous-valued control problem. The
analysis also shows that over a finite state space, the gain of binary power
control (which only takes a small number of states) is close to the extremal
gain of optimal power control, which can take any value in the interval between
the extremal gains of binary and optimal power.
  The work also shows how to upper-bound the gap between the extremal gain of
optimal power control over continuous power levels and that over a discrete (on/
off) power control, thus showing the practical effect of the theoretical
extremal analysis.
  Besides developing new tools to study continuous-control problems over
discrete-valued states, the work offers an opportunity to revisit interference
alignment (IA) in large networks, for narrowband (non-fading) wireless networks
first and extend the ideas to wideband (fading) networks later. It shows the
minimum number of stations (MSs) required to achieve optimal IA gain (comparing
fairly with a benchmark of overall interference) and the range of the spectrum
that can be saved through IA, for various network sizes. Again, the approach
offers a chance to revisit the problem of IA in wireless networks, not to
analyze interference alignment modes or gain bounds, but to study extremal
patterns of interference, thus bringing GDoF analysis closer to gDoF (granular
DoF) analysis.

$\phi$, $\Xi$ and $\Xi^*$ particles is compared to the one obtained within
standard CQM. Correlation effects in the elastic form factors of the vector
charm tetraquark $c\bar{d}$ and the beauty tetraquark $b\bar{d}$ are also
estimated. In a last part of this work the extension of the present formalism
to the case of the radiative transition form factors is outlined.
  It is shown that the correlation effects in the radiative transition form
factors are similar to the ones observed in the case of the elastic form
factors.

radiative transition form factors are directly connected to the elastic ones.

several mesons and barions.

data and to the results of other models.

understanding systems. To facilitate the future development of models that can
process negation effectively, we present CONDAQA, the first English reading
comprehension dataset which requires reasoning about the implications of
negated statements in paragraphs. We collect paragraphs with diverse negation
cues, then have crowdworkers ask questions about the implications of the
negated statement in the passage. We also have workers make three kinds of
edits to the passage -- paraphrasing the negated statement, changing the scope
of the negation, and reversing the negation -- resulting in clusters of
question-answer pairs that are difficult for models to answer with spurious
shortcuts. CONDAQA features 14,182 question-answer pairs with over 200 unique
negation cues and is challenging for current state-of-the-art models. The best
performing model on CONDAQA (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) achieves only 42% on our
consistency metric, well below human performance which is 81%. We release our
dataset, along with fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot evaluations, to
facilitate the development of future NLP methods that work on negated language.
  We study the performance of CONDAQA of few-shot and zero-shot learning models
on implicit negation implications, which are the implications of negated
statements that are not explicitly stated in the paragraph. We define an
implicit negation implication as an implication that spans two sentences
separately, i.e. an implication that cannot be implied by a single sentence.
There are 6,500 implicit negation implications out of 14,182 total implications
in CONDAQA. Few-shot and zero-shot models under-perform on implicit implications
compared to explicit implications, showing that implicit implications are a
hard task. Models that use contextualized representation learn better on implicit
implications when they are asked to answer questions about implicit
implications in few-shot settings. Graph-based methods also perform better than
plain T5 on implicit implications in zero-shot settings. Interestingly,
paraphrasing edits have a greater impact on implicit implications than scope
changes, showing that implicit implications are about coreference-based
structures that are affected by changes in reference frames.

quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we show that the minimum of the
annealing gap, which is an important bottleneck of quantum annealing
algorithms, can be revealed from a dynamical quench parameter which describes
the dynamical quantum state after the quench. Combined with statistical tools
including the training of a neural network, the relation between quench and
annealing dynamics can be exploited to reproduce the full functional behavior
of the annealing gap from the quench data. We show that the partial or full
knowledge about the annealing gap which can be gained in this way can be used
to design optimized quantum annealing protocols with a practical
time-to-solution benefit.
  From a theoretical perspective, the presented findings offer a general
theoretical framework which can be used to bridge the gap between both cases of
time evolution of a quantum system. In particular, the relation between both
scenarios may be crucial for the cases where the Hamiltonian of the system is
varied dynamically in time, e.g. in the case of dynamical quantum phase
transitions.
  We argue that the presented findings can be used as a useful tool to
validate any quantum annealing protocol, without the need for simulations of
the full time-evolution of the system. In particular, knowing the minimal
annealing gap of a device allows to compare it with the gaps of the same
Hamiltonian simulated on a suitable reference computer, which can be used to
estimate the expected performance of the device in terms of error probability
and required annealing time, up to a relevant error tolerance. This allows to
assess how important the restriction to quantum simulation is for a particular
Hamiltonian and under which conditions classical simulation is feasible. We
demonstrate the importance of such a validation in various cases of relevant
quantum annealing protocols.

observed process behavior recorded in event data. Alignments are a
state-of-the-art technique to detect, localize, and quantify deviations in
process executions, i.e., traces, compared to reference process models.
Alignments, however, assume complete process executions covering the entire
process from start to finish or prefixes of process executions. This paper
defines infix/postfix alignments, proposes approaches to their computation, and
evaluates them using real-life event data.
  Given a reference process model, an observed process behavior (or trace),
and all process traces that conform to the process model, the proposed
approaches compute all infix/postfix deviations, i.e., changes in process
behavior that indicate that a trace might deviate from the process model in
some parts of its process execution. The approaches exploit various aspects
such as process model structure, process model behavior, and event data. The
approaches are evaluated using real-life event data from the Cogent and Cogito
domains. The results verify that all infix/postfix deviations can be computed
efficiently and effectively.
  In conclusion, this paper generalizes alignment techniques to infix/postfix
alignments, proposing approaches to handle infix and postfix alignments
separately, and evaluating these approaches with real-life event data. The
proposed approaches can be used to improve conformance checking, detecting,
localizing, and quantifying process deviations from reference process models
more thoroughly.

efficient polynomial-time algorithm for finding a maximum-weight anti Tai
mapping for the case when one of the two trees is a path and further show how

criminal justice system. Using North Carolina court cases from 1994 to 2009, I
evaluate whether mental health treatment as a term of probation decreases the
likelihood that offenders return to the criminal justice system in the future.
Among offenders sentenced to probation, I compare those who were required to
seek mental health treatment to those who were not, using random variation in
judge assignment. I find that being assigned to seek mental health treatment
decreases the likelihood of three-year recidivism by 5.6 percentage points, or
17 percent. Treatment is most effective in reducing future violent and property
crimes, and the effect increases over time since conviction. A simple cost
benefit analysis suggests that the treatment-induced decrease in future crime
would be more than sufficient to offset the costs of providing treatment.
Beyond the crime reduction channel, I also consider whether mental health
treatment increases offenders' earnings and life satisfaction, although these
outcomes are harder to measure. Using social security earnings data linked to
conviction records, I find that treatment is associated with an increase in
long-term earnings among those with lower earnings prior to conviction.
Using survey data collected from Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, I find that
treatment is associated with an increase in self-reported life satisfaction at
the time of survey (typically decades) after conviction.
  Finally, I evaluate the role of mental health treatment in a generalized
matching model of the relationship between mental health treatment and crime
over the life cycle. Using rich data on mental health symptoms and treatment
status among offenders, I show that crime is negatively related to mental health
symptoms, and that this effect is primarily driven by the effect of mental
health treatment on reducing symptoms. I evaluate two identification strategies
- using variation in judge assignment and using variation in mental health
symptoms - and show that while both are valid, they yield different insights
into the causal effect of mental health treatment on crime.
  In conclusion, this work demonstrates the promise of using court records to
evaluate non-experimental programs and establishes that mental health treatment
induces a lasting decrease in crime, and likely an increase in life satisfaction
as well.

presented ten years ago at the first PxTP workshop. Since then the format has
matured. veriT proofs are used within multiple applications, and other solvers
generate proofs in the same format. We would now like to gather feedback from
the community to guide future developments. Towards this, we review the history
of the format, present our pragmatic approach to develop the format, and also
discuss problems that might arise when other solvers use the format.
  When developing the format, our main principle was to prove termination of
veriT. This led us to reject a proposal to include a form of nested proofs,
which would have extended the format, but would not be used by veriT. We also
discuss how the format deals with cuts, which are absent from the format, but
needed by other solvers.
  To further develop the format, we would like to receive feedback on several
topics. We present problems that arise when other solvers use the format,
discuss how the format could be used to prove more interesting theorems and
review in completeness of proofs produced by veriT.
  By reviewing all aspects of the format, we aim to gather a set of best
practices that could be adopted when developing proof formats in general.
  Finally, with the feedback gathered, we plan to update our proof library to
make it even more usable for developers of other solvers.
  We end by listing some open questions on proof production and consumption.
Checking proofs is an extremely efficient process, but there are still a few
cases where the checker runs out of memory. We would like to explore ways to
improve the memory usage of the proof checker.
  Overall, with this workshop, we aim to further establish proofs as a
fundamental output of SMT solvers and generally useful tool for computer
science.

paper, we investigate the role of magnetic fields in major mergers by running
high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations with the moving-mesh code
Arepo. We run MHD simulations of two major merger pairs with initial galaxy
masses of $2 \times 10^{11} {\rm M}_{\odot}$ and $2 \times 10^{12} {\rm
M}_{\odot}$, as well as comparison non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic (NIMH) and
non-magnetic simulations for comparison. We find that the magnetic field
produced in the NIMH simulations is a good indicator of the synchrotron
emission in microlensing surveys such as CMB-lensing, with magnetic field
strengthening by an order of magnitude the constraint on the star-formation
rate per unit mass from observations of the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich
effect. Analysis of the simulated galaxies suggests that magnetic fields have
an effect on gas disc fragmentation and the final morphology of the merged
galaxy.
  We find that magnetic fields enhance the likelihood of the formation of
multiple nuclei in major mergers, with this being particularly true for more
massive galaxies. Having multiple nuclei is an important characteristic of
galaxies in the core of clusters, and further regulates the global star
formation rate per unit mass. Merging galaxies are also more likely to have a
disc component which could be an ingredient for the formation of spiral
galaxies in cosmological simulations, as typically the disc is destroyed by
the collision itself. Finally, magnetic fields slow the gas outflows produced
during the merger, with this being particularly true for more massive galaxies.
This could have a profound impact on the global star formation rate, as
calculated in observations and simulations, and will be the subject of a
follow-up paper.
  Our results support the idea that magnetic fields have an important role in
the evolution of galaxies, and we encourage further studies with larger
initial galaxy masses and with the inclusion of photoionization and stellar
evolution.

change in suicide rate. In this paper, we consider rounding of rounded means,
rounded medians, and rounded least squares estimators to understand the
distributional effects of rounding on inference. We provide closed form
expressions for the distribution of the rounded estimator in these settings and
validate our expressions with simulations. We show that the effects of
rounding can be substantial and may lead to substantial losses in precision.

rounded estimator needed for robust inference under rounding.

interest is estimated using a regression type estimator and consider rounding
of the estimator both on the response and predictor scales. Once again, we
provide closed form expressions for the distribution of the rounded estimator
in this setting as well and validate our expressions with simulations. Our
work provides a general framework for analyzing the effects of rounding on
estimators of parameters as well as linear combinations of parameters and can
be used to understand losses in precision due to rounding.

expressions for the distribution of the rounded log-linear estimator. While
these expressions can be used to simulate the exact distribution of the rounded
estimator needed for robust inference under rounding, they can also be
utilized to derive approximations for the distribution of the rounded estimator
over the parameter space. We work out such an application in the special case
of inferring on rounded average suicide rates before and after a national
emergency started.

wide temperature range from 1.02 K to 2 K. The 1/3 magnetization plateau and the

  Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) is a popular method for learning deep
neural networks on labeled source data and applying them on unlabeled target
data with a different distribution. Recent work has shown that these networks
can be made more robust by applying data augmentation to the target images to
simulate the data variability in the source domain. In this work, we take a
step back and ask: "Do we really need data variability, i.e., different
underlying distributions of images, in unsupervised domain adaptation?" Our
empirical study shows that the answer is no. To demonstrate this, we introduce
two new datasets for standard UD A benchmarks, namely Adapt-Vtec and
Adapt-City. Our empirical study shows that even when there is statistically
significant evidence of a data domain shift between the source and target
datasets, simple empirical risk minimization (training the network to
minimize its error on labeled source data) yields state-of-the-art performance
on the target data. We open-source our datasets at
https://github.com/ASubhani01/UDA_B

real-time detector to search for DM-induced nuclear recoils, paleo-detectors
take advantage of small samples of naturally occurring rocks on Earth that have
been deep underground ($\gtrsim 5$ km), accumulating nuclear damage tracks from
recoiling nuclei for $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr. Modern microscopy techniques promise
the capability to read out nuclear damage tracks with nanometer resolution in
macroscopic samples. Thanks to their $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr integration times,
paleo-detectors could constitute nuclear recoil detectors with keV recoil
energy thresholds and 100 kilotonne-yr exposures. This combination would allow
paleo-detectors to probe DM-nucleon cross sections orders of magnitude below
existing upper limits from conventional direct detection experiments. In this
article, we use improved background modeling and a new spectral analysis
technique to update the sensitivity forecast for paleo-detectors. We
demonstrate the robustness of the sensitivity forecast to the (lack of)
ancillary measurements of the age of the samples and the parameters controlling
the backgrounds, systematic mismodeling of the spectral shape of the
backgrounds, and the radiopurity of the mineral samples. Specifically, we
demonstrate that even if the uranium concentration in paleo-detector samples
were to be $\x100$ higher than the current median value, the sensitivity of a
single paleo-detector would still exceed the existing upper limits from
direct detection experiments on the full range of DM masses for which
paleo-detectors are designed to probe, and the forecasted sensitivity would be
only slightly reduced.

intervention used to examine the
organs inside the abdomen and has been widely used due to its effectiveness
over open surgery. Due to the hardware improvements such as high definition
cameras, this procedure has significantly improved and new software methods
including computer vision have been adopted to enhance the accuracy and
effectiveness of procedures. However, there are still challenges and
imperfections during such surgeries, some of which are beyond human
capabilities such as motion prediction, injury detection, and blood flow
analysis. Computer vision methods have been used for these purposes, but there
is a need for evaluation metrics to assess these techniques more effectively
and accurately. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of the
application of computer vision in laparoscopic surgery and propose a taxonomy
for the evaluation of computer vision techniques used in such procedures. We
present the common challenges and inferences drawn during such procedures and
emphasize the importance of standardization of data sets used for training and
testing. Finally, we propose a framework of a unified metric to evaluate and
compare the performance of various computer vision methods used in laparoscopic
surgeries.
  From a practical perspective, our work has the potential of leading to
improvements in the accuracy and effectiveness of procedures, ultimately
resulting in better patient care. From a theoretical perspective, our work has
the potential of leading to the development of new algorithms and the
improvement of existing ones, ultimately leading to a unified metric for
evaluation.
  The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present
the common computer vision applications and tools used in laparoscopic surgeries
including image acquisition, injury detection, blood flow analysis, and
taskanalysis. In Section 3, we present the advantages and disadvantages of the
techniques used in acquiring images from the laparoscope, followed by a
discussion on the essential considerations for the installation of such
systems. In Section 4, we present a review of segmentation techniques used in
the context of laparoscopic surgeries, followed by a discussion on the
important factors in the evaluation of such methods. In Section 5, we present
a review of registration techniques used in laparoscopic surgeries, followed by
a discussion on the important factors in the evaluation of such methods. In
Section 6, we present a review of action recognition techniques used in
laparoscopic surgeries, followed by a discussion on the important factors in the
evaluation of such approaches.

redistribution decisions from a U.S.-representative sample who observe worker

participants redistribute less and are less reactive to changes in the

implications for models that seek to understand and predict redistribution

simplification of the policy intervention of offering a lucky opportunity to a
low-income worker, by comparing outcomes to a counterfactual scenario in which
the opportunity would have been offered to a average-income worker. We show that
standard approaches to policy evaluation under lucky opportunities will
overstate the benefits of antipoverty interventions that create lucky
opportunities, and understate the benefits of those that remove them. We
illustrate the magnitude of this bias using data from the United States and
findings from the literature on job mobility.
  Finally, we study how people reinterpret information about luck and inequality
as they learn about the mechanisms generating inequality. We study two
developing democracies, Ghana and Tanzania, using lists of wealthy individuals
with information about their occupation, industry, and how long they have been
in their position. We find that respondents are skeptical that luck has
played little role in determining the wealth of these individuals; that is,
respondents on average estimate that at least half of the wealth of these
individuals is due to luck. We show that this skepticism is largely explained
by respondents' perception that these individuals have not made effort to
acquire wealth (e.g. by working hard or investing in education or business
initiatives). That is, respondents' estimates of the role of luck are highly
correlated with their judgments about whether these individuals are
opportunistically taking advantage of lucky opportunities.

poor. We find strong evidence that as wealth concentration in the population
increases, people become less supportive of redistribution and less

which one fundamental challenge is to understand the influence of data quality
to ML training -- "Which training examples are 'guilty' in making the trained
ML model predictions inaccurate or unfair?" Modeling data influence for ML
training has attracted intensive interest over the last decade, and one popular
line of work views each training example as a "vote" to define data
influence. Unfortunately, existing works do not consider data representation
abuse and the privacy of training data, which are essential in large-scale ML
applications. Moreover, they cannot be scaled to accommodate the massive training
data that modern ML applications typically involve. In this paper, we introduce
a new formulation of private influence measurement called Pricay that is
computationally efficient, private against the training data owners, and
applicable to any ML training procedure. Pricay only requires the trained ML
model and one example-wise additional data access per training example. The
resulting influence graph is scalable, private, and suitable for downstream
ML analysis such as feature influence analysis and adversarial attack
identification.
  We show that our formulation can produce privately influenced feature
maps. In addition, the data influencing the ML model can be identified by
projecting the privately influenced feature maps onto original training data.
We show that our projection scheme has a linear time complexity and is
scalable. We also show that our influence measurement is suitable for
adversarial analysis by using an isolation boundary constructed by aggregating
privately influenced features. Evaluations on four ML datasets and four
adversarial scenarios show the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach.

multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step
toward the deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world applications.
However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has a different level of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, jeopardizing the
performance of the entire team. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL with
explicit consideration on the diversity of agent-wise trajectories and propose
a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to address this
problem. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network assigns
the credit to each agent through a differentiable key-value memory mechanism in
an offline manner. These decomposed credits are then used to reconstruct the
joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with individual
trajectories, thereafter agents can share their good trajectories and
conservatively train their policies with a graph attention network (GAT) based
critic. We evaluate our method in both discrete control (i.e., StarCraft II and
multi-agent particle environment) and continuous control (i.e, multi-agent
mujoco). The results indicate that our method achieves significantly better
results in complex and mixed offline MARL scenarios.
  We propose a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) for
multi-agent reinforcement learning, in which attention-based reward
decomposition network assigns the credit to each agent through a differentiable
key-value memory mechanism, and the graph attention network (GAT) based critic
reconstructs the joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with
individual trajectories.
  The key-value memory mechanism makes the credit assignment depend on the
history of the joint trajectory, making the reward better suited to the
scenario. In addition, our framework specifies how to use the reward function
in an offline setting through experience priorization, which helps agents to
share their good trajectories and conservatively train their policies.

it easier to add or remove agents from a reward designed for a scenario with a
fixed number of agents.

reaction of Tl with neutrons produced by neutron source is focused onto the

 diameter of 30 cm. The control system can control whole process of neutron,

profile of the scintillation signal of GECAM GRDs triggered by the device

  a novel hybrid-dimensional model of single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured
porous media. In this model, the fracture is treated as an $(d-1)$-dimensional
interface within the $d$-dimensional fractured porous domain, for $d=2, 3$. Two
classes of fracture are distinguished based on the permeability magnitude ratio
between the fracture and its surrounding medium: when the permeability in the
fracture is (significantly) larger than in its surrounding medium, it is
considered as a {\it conductive} fracture; when the permeability in the
fracture is (significantly) smaller than in its surrounding medium, it is
considered as a {\it blocking} fracture. The conductive fractures are treated
using the classical hybrid-dimensional approach of the interface model where
pressure is assumed to be continuous across the fracture interfaces, while the
blocking fractures are treated using the recent Dirac-$\delta$ function
approach where normal component of Darcy velocity is assumed to be continuous
across the interface. Due to the use of Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for
the blocking fractures, our numerical scheme allows for nonconforming meshes
with respect to the blocking fractures. A novel hybrid-mixed formulation is
developed for solving the system of nonlinear equations arising from the
discretization of the model. A priori error estimate is proved. Numerical
results verify the convergence of the numerical solution, verify the consistency
of the model with the classical interface model when all the fractures are
treated as conductive fractures, and illustrate the impact of the blocking
fractures on the pressure and flux fields.

sembles of coupled oscillators map
to different functional states in a wide range of applications, e.g., active
and resting states in the brain and stable and unstable power grid
configurations. For this reason, explosive synchronization transitions, which
facilitate sharp, continuous maping between functional states and ensemble
behavior have recently garnered significant interest. While previous work has
identified explosive transitions in dynamical systems with explicit disorder,
to date, existing analyses of related non-disordered systems are not general
and apply only to specific architectures. Here, we extend previous work to
include a wide class of architectures and provide a general characterization
of the explosive transition in a prototype architecture, the Kuramoto network
with nonlinear local dynamics.
  We find that an explosive transition is possible if the degree of each
node, the strength of the mean-field and the strength of the connections between
distant nodes all fall within a certain range. If any of these parameters
exceeds a critical value an abrupt transition is suppressed. If all fall below
a second, higher critical value, the transition is also not suppressed, but is
instead smoothed out. Therefore, the range of parameters over which an explosive
transition is possible is directly controlled by the ratio between the two
critical values. Across different architectures, however, the specific relation
between the degree of the nodes and the transition type depends on the specific
dynamics used. Finally, we show that an explosive transition is sufficient to
generate a wide class of complex behaviors from basic nonlinear local dynamics.
In particular, the hyperchaos observed in the Chua circuit is generated by the
simple attraction to a bi-stable state in the prototype architecture.
Moreover, the explosive transition itself is crucial to the generation of a
sharp blink-neon flash transition in a network modeling the human visual
system.
  In conclusion, an explosive synchronization transition is a general feature
of coupled oscillator networks, provided by a necessary condition for which the
specific dynamics becomes irrelevant. It has to be investigated when studying
any new architecture, and it can be used to generate a wide range of complex
functional states.

Reversi game. Here, we address the question whether a single algorithm can
play different types of Reversi games. The algorithm encodes one set of rules
that determine which actions are available and their costs. From an external
point of view, we can define different game definitions by selecting which
rules are active. Thus, multiple games can be seen as an instance of a
higher-level problem, from which the individual games emerge. In experiments,
we show that a single algorithm can play several types of Reversi games,
including the well-known Endgame style Reversi, which won the second
International Online Reversi Tournament in 2003. Our results indicate that
state-of-the-art evolutionary algorithms for Reversi play a focused game with
very few opening moves. In contrast, our approach is able to play a variety of
different games while still achieving a high level of playing performance.
Finally, the present approach may be transferred to other board games that
exhibit similar characteristics.

metric called the depth of an algorithm, which measures the layering of the
selection and genetic operations in evolutionary algorithms. Second, we show

an inverse problem with high accuracy by effectively emulating the performance of

the sensing matrix. Our results provide a general theoretical framework for
exploring the relationship between NNs and optimal estimators in inverse problems
and can be used to guide the design of more effective NNs for compressed
sensing and related problems.

Central Bank and European Commission, is widely used in the modern financial
markets. It is an agreement between a group of market participants, which can
be counterparties, to net their trades with each other. The aim is to reduce
the number of the actual payments (the `ultimate netting amount') while
ensuring the financial stability by providing collateral and guarantee
conditions. In this paper we present a combinatorial model for the netting
problem in three-stage framework (before, during, and after the settlement)
including the role of a central counterparty. We address the problem of
designing such an agreement among the participants in two different optimization
studies. In the first study our objective is to minimize the sum of the
payment/default risk for the agreement. In the second study, however, our aim is
to distribute the netting amount among the participants in a fair manner while
minimizing the sum of the default costs for the agreement. Both studies
resulting from our model are studied computationally for large-scale instances.
We also present heuristic approaches for solving the studied problems in
real-time. We present an upper bound analysis with regard to exact-upper bound
and lower bound computations. We show that all our computational studies
resulting from the exact and heuristic approaches are of order of seconds or
minutes, depending on the problem size.

from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb collisions in terms of final-state multiplicity.
The study of Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions allows systems at similar
charged-particle multiplicities but with different initial geometrical
eccentricities to be investigated. A detailed comparison of the spectral shapes
in the two systems reveals an opposite behaviour for radial and elliptic flow.
In particular, this study shows that the radial flow does not depend on the
colliding system when compared at similar charged-particle multiplicity. In
terms of hadron chemistry, the previously observed smooth evolution of particle
ratios with multiplicity from small to large collision systems is also found to
hold in Xe-Xe. In addition, our results confirm that two remarkable features of
particle production at LHC energies are also valid in the collision of
medium-sized nuclei: the lower proton-to-pion ratio with respect to the thermal
model expectations and the increase of the $\phi$-to-pion ratio with increasing
final-state multiplicity.
  Finally, because the present data exhibit a superior signal-over-noise ratio
with respect to previous measurements, we have compared the transverse momentum
distributions of pions, kaons, protons and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb
collisions at similar multiplicity, up to $p_{\rm T}~100$ GeV/$c$. The
agreement between the two systems is excellent when taking into account the
different nuclear geometries and initial elliptic eccentricities. Such an
excellent agreement is ideal for the study of QCD at the Kolmogorov scale.
  The results reported here have been obtained using the ALICE experiment at the
LHC in Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV.

reported and compared to measurements in other nuclei-nuclei collisions and

dataset has greatly boosted the research on dialogue state
tracking (DST). However, substantial noise has been discovered in its state
annotations. Such noise brings about huge challenges for training DST models
robustly. Although several recent studies have investigated the noise in the
MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset, they all focus on a specific aspect of the noise and
proposed solutions to it. In this paper, we take a general approach to
understand the noise in the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset automatically. We train a
state-of-the-art DST model on different subsets of the dataset with varying
levels of strictness during data generation. Our experiment shows that the
model performance does not improve when more "correct" data is included, which
means there is still a large amount of hidden noise in the dataset. With the
model output as an indicator of the similarity of states, we further
characterize the noise in the dataset, such as the close-but-not-the-same
states, which is also a challenge for natural language processing. We also
identify the source of the noise from the annotation guidelines and the
annotation process. To reduce the noise, we propose a new data generation
strategy: from general to specific. We evaluate the effectiveness of our
strategy by comparing it with the current approach used in MultiWOZ 2.0. Our
experiment shows that our approach improves the model performance on the
validation set significantly while keeping the test set performance almost the
same. Besides, our approach reduces the number of unnecessary states by 18%.
Moreover, it makes the current data augmentation strategy more efficient. In
summary, we identify the hidden noise in the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and propose
effective methods to reduce it automatically.
  Which states are similar and should be merged? How to avoid adding
unnecessary states during state merging? These are two major challenges for
state merging, especially in a dataset with noise. In the dialogue state
tracking community, the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has been widely used as a benchmark
for evaluating the performance of state merging. However, during the state
merging in the dataset development, both of the above questions are addressed
heuristically. In this paper, we study them from a data quality perspective.
First, we propose a method to learn the similarity metric for states automatically. However, the
models trained on the validation data do not work well on the test data as
state mergers.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough for real-world scenarios. We propose LIOFAR (Learning Inertial-Visual
Odometry in a Self-Modulating Fashion), a novel end-to-end learning-inference
framework for VIO, which integrates a recurrent frontier model with a signal
processing module activated by a self-modulating mask. The signal processing
module allows direct integration of raw visual and inertial signals without
needing feature extraction, while the recurrent frontier model enables flexible
and efficient signal processing. Compared to existing learning based VIO
approaches, our model is easier to train and provides better performance in
real-world scenarios. For example, our evaluation on the KITTI dataset shows
that LIOFAR achieves an average translation REPEATER error of 0.57 meter, out
performing LEVO (a recent learning based VIO baseline) by 0.08 meter.
  We make the following contributions: We propose a novel end-to-end learning
inference framework for VIO, which integrates recurrent model with signal
processing. The signal processing activated by a self-modulating mask allows
direct integration of raw visual and inertial signals without feature
extraction. Compared to existing learning based VIO approaches, our model is
easier to train and provides better performance in real-world scenarios.

knowledge-amalgamation problem, termed
Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and should also be distinct
from the target task. A major challenge in FedSA is to resolve the task
disalignment between teachers and the student. To this end, we propose a
co-training framework that partitions the feature space based on the teachers'
tasks and models their shared knowledge within each partition. To facilitate
data distribution awareness, we further develop a discriminative graph to
model the data-related similarity between the teachers. An intrinsic challenge
in the proposed framework is to determine the optimal set of teachers and the
relevant student parameters. To this end, we formulate a principled optimization
framework that adapts the teachers to the student while respecting the
teachers' distinct tasks and feature space partitions. Experimental results on
multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSA.
  We also study a new flow minimization problem, termed Minimum Flow
Aggregation (MFA), of combining the decentralized flow-generating models
fitted under different tasks Fitting a model to fit data is natural and
important but, to our knowledge, has received little attention in the context
of flow conservation. The challenge is to aggregate the decentralized models
while respecting the distinct tasks and the flow conservation law. A naive
solution is to wait for the global optimizer that solves the related
least-squares problem despite the necessity of a large amount of communication.
An alternative, efficient, communication-reduced solution is to employ
recent progress in federated learning, e.g., federated averaging. However, it
is still unclear how to conduct the data-aware optimization that adapts the
minimization of the total flow to the data distributions. To this end, we
propose a general framework, termed Data-Aware Minimum Flow Aggregation
(DA-MFA), which optimizes either the total flow or the weighted total flow.
The proposed framework is shown to cover the recently proposed methods as
their special cases and is equipped with the data reuse awareness through the
discriminative graph construction.

solar age, approximately following the empirical Skumanich's law and enabling

the braking action of magnetic winds and the boosting effect of internal dynamo
action. The characterization of younger solar-type stars requires empirical
laws of global rotation vs. age and mass, which are needed to constrain
stellar models. Such laws can also be used to control the exaggeration of the
solar spin down induced by excessive youthfully fast rotation in studied examples
like Kepler-16B and TRAPPIST-1. To obtain direct measurements during the main
sequence, we looked for asteroseismically identified solar-type stars with
rotation determined from their internal dynamics. Twenty stars with
well-characterized ages, masses, and evolutionary stages were selected. Among
them, we found a clear correlation between the dimensionless characteristic
rotation rate $v_{eq}/v_{c}$ and the stellar age $t$ of the form
$v_{eq}/v_{c}\propto t^b$, with $b\approx0.362$. This result confirms that the
decrease in global rotation follows a power law during the main sequence and

rotation at any age can be written as a sum of two laws: a power-law representing

evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics of research. Observations of rocks in crustal
exposures at Venusian volcanoes provide a window into the planet's paleo-

potentially habitable early state to the hot, acidic world it is today. A
critical question is the extent to which Venus's surface environment has
variied over billions of years. We also discuss timescales for exchange of
gases between Venus's atmosphere and interior, with implications for tracking
of gases generated or consumed by interior processes. Finally, we consider how
the evolution of atmospheric composition has influenced climate evolution,
linking to surface temperature and radiative balance.

formation, which suggests habitable conditions may have existed on Venus in the

as natural disasters, online message exchanges, financial transactions or
neuronal spike trains. One very popular point process model in which the
probability of occurrences of new events depend on the past of the process is
the Hawkes process. In this work we consider the nonlinear Hawkes process,
which generalises the Hawkes process in such a way that the log-amplitude of
the kernel is a function of the time between events and their marks (additional
data attached to the events). This generalisation allows for transversal
instabilities in the process, which imply burst phenomena which are commonly
observed in real data. Fitting such a model to data is challenging due to the
lack of explicit solutions for the likelihood function. In this work we present
an efficient method for log-likelihood computation based on stochastic gradient
descent. We further prove convergence results for the estimator. As an
application of the model, we work on an example dataset of Twitter messages
generated by accounts of an English football club. The results show the ability
of the model to capture bursts in Twitter data triggered by unexpected events
such as losses in football games.

nonlinearity to the time-dependent amplitude of the nonlinear Hawkes process.
Second, we introduce a new efficient algorithm for maximum likelihood
estimation. Third, we introduce a new framework to evaluate the performance of
such models on social media datasets via feature extraction and classification.
In addition, the surge of an event can be connected to the magnitude of the
burst, for example measured as the number of messages per minute, and can be
differentiated from the baseline activity of the account, which can be equated
to the steady state of the process. We propose a method based on features
derived from patterns of bursts and a probabilistic threshold selection
methodology in order to extract anomalies indicating unexpected events from
Twitter data.

point processes, namely the nonlinear Hawkes process, for online event
detection. The organization of the work follows a data-driven perspective and
provides a self-contained example of how to fit such a model to a real dataset
and how to connect the bursts of an example social media platform to
extrinsic anomalous events.

annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) methods are promising
to reduce the requirement of annotations, but their performance is still
limited when the dataset size and the number of annotated images are small.
Leveraging existing annotated datasets with similar anatomical structures to
assist training has a potential for improving the model's performance. However,
it is further challenged by the cross-anatomy domain shift due to the different
appearance and even imaging modalities from the target structure. To solve this
problem, we propose Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy
Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that adapts a model to segment similar structures
in a new domain with the help of existing annotated datasets in other domains.
CS-CADA is a new SSL framework that adapts to the cross-anatomy domain shift.
The key idea is to use contrastive learning to exploit both labeled and
unlabeled training images as well as transfer knowledge from source domains to
the target domain. We design a domain-adaptive contrastive loss function that
fuses two types of transitions: camera transition and anatomy transition. The
latter is specific to medical imaging and has never been explored in SSL. We
divide transitions into camera transitions (modality transition, pose
transition, and view transition) and anatomy transitions ( anatomy transfer
across domains). Extensive experiments show that our CS-CADA achieves
state-of-the-art performance on four publicly available medical segmentation
datasets.

consider camera transition (e.g., modality transition, view transition, pose

transitions for cross-anatomy domain shift adaptation. We propose a unified
contrastive loss containing camera transition and anatomy transition for state-of-the-art
medical segmentation models to adapt to the real-world domain shift. The
key idea is to use contrastive learning to exploit both labeled and unlabeled
training images as well as transfer knowledge from source domains to the target
domain. A careful analysis of our loss function shows that the attribution of
the gain in performance comes from the anatomy transition, indicating the
importance of anatomy transition for cross-anatomy domain shift. Extensive

used as a simple toy model to look at the BRS symmetry of the first, second and

analyzed in detail, in a simple model, where easy calculations are available,
the 1.5 formalism always generates an invalid BRS operator, which is not even
nilpotent. This clearly is also the case for supergravity. It follows that a
revised and completed set of nilpotent first order supergravity transformations
is needed to properly understand 3+1 dimensional supergravity. Such a set seems
easy to write down, by simply adding two more auxiliary fields so that the spin
connection becomes part of a super--YM multiplet.
  The relevant part of the supergravity 1.5 transformation algebra, obtained by
selecting only the physical degrees of freedom, is reconsidered. It is shown
that, in general, it does not even possess a deformation of nilpotency.
  Nilpotent 3+1 dimensional consistent (massless) (super--)Wess--Zumino
theories do not exist, unless one considers (super--)non-commutative WZ theories
obtained by lifting (massless) (super--)Yang--Mills theories to the
non-commutative space. In this way, the Fierz--Pauli five parameter
deformation of massless Duff--Gibbons--Rowan Horowitz--Strominger descending
from the volume form of tori becomes the product of the five parameters, as it
should, and not their sum, as it happens in 5d (super--)YM.
  The 1.5 order formalism is revisited. It is shown that, in general, the
1.5 order formalism always generates an invalid BRS operator, which is not even
nilpotent. This clearly is also the case for supergravity. A simple way to
overcome the flaw of the 1.5 formalism is obtained by promoting the auxiliary
fields of supergravity to physical fields. This gives a new set of nilpotent
first order supergravity transformations.

confidence. We propose Selective Labeling to simplify the labeling process by
providing an auxiliary to assist the labeler with relevant information while
increasing the volume of labeled data available for training. At any point in
the labeling process, we use an extraction model to generate predictions on a
small subset of the documents. We then use the model's mistakes -- the documents
that the model gets wrong -- as input to the labeling process. The extraction
model is trained on all labeled documents, including those labeled with the
auxiliary's assistance as well as those labeled after the model's predictions
are considered. We show that even a small number of labeled documents (e.g.
400) with the auxiliary's assistance can be better than a large number of
labeled documents (e.g., 4000) without the auxiliary.

model is most uncertain about, instead of relying on the model's mistakes.
While this can significantly reduce the number of labels needed to reach a
particular performance level, it does not significantly outperform random
sampling on the documents to label.
  Finally, we show that the model trained with labeled documents identified by
the auxiliary performs better on a "cold start" scenario -- where we start with a
new set of documents to label instead of continuing from the set labeled in the
training data -- than a model trained on all 4000 documents without any
assistance. Thus the strategy not only increases the volume of labeled data but
also improves the robustness of the model.

trained to extract different types of information from invoices.

-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and Virgo
Interferometer Collaborations have now detected all three classes of compact
binary mergers: binary black hole (BBH), binary neutron star (BNS), and neutron
star-black hole (NSBH). For coalescences involving neutron stars, the
simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation
produced by an event, has broader potential to enhance our understanding of
these events, and also to probe the equation of state (EOS) of dense matter.
However, electromagnetic follow-up to gravitational wave (GW) events requires
rapid real-time detection and classification of GW signals, and conventional
detection approaches are computationally prohibitive for the anticipated rate
of detection of next-generation GW detectors. In this work, we present the
first deep learning based results of classification of GW signals from NSBH
mergers in \textit{real} LIGO data. We show for the first time that a deep
neural network can successfully distinguish all three classes of compact binary
mergers and separate them from detector noise. Specifically, we train a
convolutional neural network (CNN) on $\sim 500,000$ data samples of real LIGO
noise with injected BBH, BNS, and NSBH GW signals, and we show that our network
has high sensitivity and accuracy. Most importantly, we successfully recover
two events from \textit{real} LIGO data with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of
$\sim 10$ and $\sim 8$, respectively, which further affirm the
predictiveness of our deep learning approach to real data.
Furthermore, we present an example of how we can narrow down the sky location
of a hypothetical future NSBH event to $\sim 100 \,\mathrm{deg}^2$ using just
10~seconds of GW data from next-generation GW detectors.
Finally, we stress that our successful results on real data attest to the
powerful astrophysical utility of deep learning approaches to enhance our
ability to detect and characterize all three classes of compact binary
mergers, which in turn will greatly increase the likelihood of identifying
associated electromagnetic counterparts.

specific instances that disagree with the predicted output, and to
generalize from those specific examples to a broader set of data. Generalization

challenge, and I argue that current models do not get enough opportunities to
learn from high-quality work that human annotators can do. I argue that there
are three key components to diagnostics: (1) identifying specific examples
that disagree with the predicted output, (2) building a narrative about why
an example is an outlier, and (3) generalizing from the narrative to a
broader set of data. Once I have completed the first two components for a
dataset of images of people who are either wearing glasses or a smile, I will
discuss how I use the narrative to generalize to a broader set of data.

a subset of the data that is causing a model to mispredict the attribute
"female", and I will discuss how I would use the narrative to write additional
textual annotations to help a model learn the difference between "smile" and
"laugh".

in the data annotation to a specific millisecond in time, enabling me to
enrich the corresponding textual annotations with additional information
with the goal of obtaining perfect performance on the validation set. From a
model perspective, the narrative allows me to diagnose mistakes of a model
and to get insights into the data by identifying relevant factors such as
concept of interest, attributes, and emotions, which are related to the
prediction task at hand. Moreover, the structure of the narrative allows

Variables (CV), known as asynchronous
polars, are still relatively poorly understood. An asynchronous polar is a
polar in which the spin period of the white dwarf is either shorter or longer
than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.
  We also find that the spectral difference is primarily driven by a few
individual sources. When we consider only those sources observed with both
ROSAT and Chandra, the difference in spectral shape is not significant.
Interestingly, the sources that stand out as having harder spectra are those
with the strongest magnetic fields (tested at the 2% level using a Kolmogorov-
Smirnov test). This result suggests that field may play a role in spectral
hardening, but that other factors must be considered when examining large
samples.
  Based upon our results, we discuss the various theories for asynchronous
polars and suggest additional observations that could help to further understand
this mysterious subclass of polar.

gives the correct results, if one considers an effective gap width $2k_F d$,

experiment. Changing the relative orientation of the magnetic moments in this

possibly even the design of magnetic and superconducting nanostructures with
prescribed spectral properties.

for horizontally homogeneous clouds. A promising approach for treating clouds
as fully 3D objects is the Cloud-Resolving Model (CRM) 1D RT, which allows
retrieving cloud optical effects directly from satellite imagery. However, the
CRM 1D RT does not account for the sub-grid cloud variability (SGCV), which
can distort the satellite measurements. Moreover, its resolution (typically 500
-1000 m) is still too coarse to resolve the morphology of convective clouds.
To address these two issues, we propose a two-step approach. First, upscaling
scales the high-resolution 3D cloud fields from the simulation to the CRM
resolution, accounting for SGCV. This allows us to construct a 3D cloud
structure that is not simply a superposition of individual 3D clouds but
represents a true multi-scale system. Then CRM 1D RT is applied on vertical
throughputings, with the upscaled 3D optical thickness and effective particle
size being input to the CRM 1D RT. Finally, a forward operator based on the
upscaled 3D cloud fields and 1D outputs converts the 1D cloud optical
properties into simulated satellite observations in satellite native
orientation and resolution. This allows evaluating 3D cloud retrievals on
satellite imagery. In this study, we test our approach on up-scaled high-resolution
3D cloud fields derived from direct numerical simulations of idealized deepening
convective clouds. We show that the upscaled 3D cloud fields reproduce well
the underlying high-resolution fields, including their variability and
occurrence of large cloud volumes. Furthermore, we show that, based on
satellite observations simulated from the 1D CRM RT outputs, traditional 1D
retrieval schemes fail to recover the convective cloud properties whereas a
recent 3D retrieval scheme works well, demonstrating the necessity of 3D
retrievals for passive satellite imagers. Finally, we show that the
retrieval performance is tied to the underlying 3D cloud fields and that
scaling the high-resolution 3D cloud fields is crucial for 3D cloud
retrievals from passive satellite imagery at CRM resolution.

problem: given a fixed finite graph $F$, what is the largest value of $\lambda$
such that every 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ contains

older upper bound. For the particular case where $F$ is a triangle, we also
give an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}=0.62203\dots$, improving

the largest value of $\lambda$ such that every 2-edge-coloring of the complete
graph on $\mathbb{N}$ contains a monochromatic infinite path whose vertex set

electron-positron spin and photon polarization effects, we investigate a

the positron yield becomes appreciable with the laser intensity exceeding

polarization is attributed to the asymmetrical laser fields positrons undergo
in the skin layer of overdense plasma, where the radiative spin-flip and

various applications.

produced if the laser intensity is too low, even if the laser field is strong
enough to initiate QED processes. This is because an too-low-density plasma
has a large skin depth, leading to symmetric field fluctuations in the
positron-radial direction, thus suppressing the positron yield. Therefore,
ensuring sufficient positron yield, i.e., $\geq 1\%$, becomes crucial for
future laser-solid experiments in the strong-field QED regime.

studies of a large variety of systems, ranging from statistical physics over

this approach relies on the derivation of so-called flow equations, which
describe the change of the quantum effective action under the variation of a
coarse-graining parameter. In the present work, we discuss in detail a novel
approach to solve such flow equations. This approach relies on the fact that RG
equations can be rewritten such that they exhibit similarities with the
conservation laws of fluid dynamics. This observation can be exploited in
different ways. First of all, we show that this allows to employ powerful
numerical techniques developed in the context of fluid dynamics to solve RG
equations. In particular, it allows us to reliably treat the emergence of
nonanalytic behavior in the RG flow of the effective action as it is expected
to occur in studies of, e.g., spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the
analogies between RG equations and fluid dynamics can provide valuable insights
into the RG flow itself. This can be achieved by casting the RG equations into
a suitable fluid-dynamical form such that the RG flow can be interpreted as an
irreversible fluid flow, which can be studied directly. As this makes use of
the mathematics of fluid dynamics it can provide valuable insights into the RG
flow itself. We demonstrate the applicability of this approach in different
cases. Throughout the paper, we focus on the two-time RG approach. The one-time
approach can be treated in the same way, see e.g. papers on the subject.
Suitable identities allowing the rewriting of one-time RG equations in a form
suitable for the application of fluid-dynamical techniques are found in the same way as for the two-time case. The main difference between the one-time and two-time approaches lies in the fact that the one-time RG equations can be rewritten in a way such that they directly exhibit similarities to Euler's fluid dynamics, while the two-time derivation follows closer to the Navier-Stokes equation. formation and destruction in the cloud center is balanced, or the destruction

cores towards the cloud center results in an enhanced core mass function
towards the cloud center.

connected, and the rotation of the cloud is determined by the angular momentum
of the cores and the torque in the centrifugal barrier.

and global effects of mass dependence on concentration and extent. The effects
are likely caused by core evolution and star formation dynamics in the cloud,
and are useful for further statistical and modeling studies.

We visually show that three distinct friction regimes exists: slippage,
stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Our stress measurements are
validated for slippage and anchored regimes based on existing models, and we
propose a leverage rule to describe the stresses during the stick-slip regime.

by the roughness factor, defined as the ratio between the size of the surface
asperities and the radius of curvature of the Plateau borders.

to slippage with a reduced viscosity. The supermm roughness leads to slippage
with an increased viscosity, and up to a critical value beyond which slippage
vanishes and anchored films are obtained. The critical roughness factor is
found to be similar to the Bond number in capillary flows, indicating that
surface tension and gravity balance the pressure difference along the
asperities. This balance explains the existence of a maximum in the averaged
friction, and the transition from stick-slip to anchored motion.

tension, and opens the route for a statistical description of complex interfaces

of an elastic membrane
separating two fluids of different density under external pressure in a
rotating Hele-Shaw cell. Both inextensible and highly extensible membranes are
considered, and the role of rotation is found to be both stabilising and
destabilising depending on the external pressure.
  In the inextensible case (with self-contact), both rigid (Taylor) and
flexible (Fabri--Poiiseuille) boundary conditions are considered. Under
rigid boundary conditions, the Taylor deformation leads to a suppression of
fingering that would otherwise occur in a nonrotating cell. Under flexible
boundary conditions, both Taylor and Fabri--Poiiseuve (slipping) deformations
are possible, and we obtain the critical values of external pressure that
induce flux reversal (upon increasing the pressure from zero) and a loss of
stability leading to flexible Taylor-like depressions and Fabri--Poiiseuille
like ripples.
  In the highly extensible case (negligible elastic energy compared to
viscous and surface energies), analysis shows that both rigid and flexible
boundaries admit a supersaturated state leading to a large buildup of
asymmetry before the steady-state is reached. Both subsystems (i.e., the
membrane and the two-fluid system) are needed to explain the instability
observed in numerical simulations starting from a symmetric initial
condition. Numerical simulations also show that, in the case of slipping
boundaries, a secondary instability occurs at the tip of the growing
asymmetry, leading to a nonlocal interaction between the tip and the
background, which could lead to a collapse of the distance between the tip
and the wall.
  Both the steady-state and the numerical aspects of this work are unexpected
and are motivated by the lack of an efficient, purely analytical, approach to
the problem. It is not clear a priori why numerical simulations with
approximate both for the membrane energy and for the hydrodynamic friction
exhibit such unexpected behaviour, suggesting that a rigorous mathematical
model is needed.
  Finally, it is worth noting that the assumption of quasi-steady flow made
here does not hold when the membrane velocity is of the order of the rotation
velocity or larger. This should be addressed in future work, particularly in
view of the observed numerical instabilities for large slipping velocities
reported here.

nonequilibrium thermodynamics to study expansion/contraction processes. Here,
the numbers of initial and final microstates are different so they cannot be
connected by unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This commonly happens when the
phase space volume changes, and has not been studied so far using Hamiltonian
trajectories that can be inverted to yield an identity mapping between initial
and final microstates as the parameter in the Hamiltonian is changed. We
propose a trick to overcome this hurdle with a focus on free expansion in an
isolated system, where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The trick
is shown to be thermodynamically consistent and can be extremely useful in
simulation. We justify that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork done by a microstate that is dissipated; this microwork is different
from the exchange microwork with the vacuum, which vanishes. We also establish
that the microwork is nonnegative for free expansion, which is remarkable,
since its sign is not fixed in a general process.
  Our approach can also be applied to a system where the environment plays a
minor role, e.g., the solid wall, where the micowork can be large and
nonnegative, indicating the nonzero heat transfer due to the thermal
fluctuations despite the macroscopically zero heat in the system.
  Finally, we propose a simple method to experimentally observe the micowork in
a expanding He gas. Our study provides a general framework of the thermodynamic
analysis of free expansion processes from the micro- to macro-scales.
Moreover, the framework can be extended to other expanding systems.
  The proposed method can be applied to the study of the quantum micowork in
expansions driven by the difference of temperature, e.g., the usual
Loschmidt's reversal, and to the thermaclogical flips which are related to the
contractions.

inequality in quasi-static, nonequilibrium, and nonadiabatic processes.
Moreover, the micowork can play an important role in the heat transfer through
the interfaces in the case of non-zero micowork.

statistical perspective of the evolution of the system from an initial to a

outcomes inspired the new discipline of translational medicine, in which the
application of new knowledge is an explicit part of a research plan. Abramson
and Parashar argue that a similar gap between complex computational
technologies and ever-more-complex biological models necessitates an
explicit attention to translation in computational biology. They define
translational computation as efficient bidirectional flow of ideas between
biology and computer science, proposing a general framework for translation
inference from sequence and structure to function and phenotype. They
illustrate how translatonal analysis can help to refine alignment methods and
evolutionary models. The framework can be applied to any problem in computational
biology, from motif discovery to protein design.
  We propose the Translational Score T(s) given by the sum of the one-way
inference scores in both directions: s = f(b) + b(f), where b and f denote the
input (e.g., sequence) and output (e.g., function) of a computational procedure
and s is the overall quality of the procedure. Inference scores measure the
plausibility of the connections between the input and output determined by
domain expertise. The application of the translational framework depends on the
specific biological problem at hand and requires minimal additional computation.
For alignment, the translational score can be used to evaluate the quality of
an alignment procedure as well as to refine alignment methods. It offers a
general framework for studying alignment procedures that takes into account the
complexity of modern genomics but has not received broad attention yet.
Furthermore, translational scores can be used to infer evolutionary relationships
between organisms by optimizing mutual understanding of genome sequence and
phylogenetic profile.
  The framework can be extended to any level of biological organization and
inference between any pairs of biological and computational representation of
life.
  Finally, translatonal analysis provides a means to reason about computation
through its biological interpretation and vice versa. This is important for
avoiding detours such as the development of supercomputers for the simulation
of protein folding, and for ensuring that the development of computational
methods is guided by the right questions from biology.
  In the long run, translatonal analysis may become an integral part of
computational biology, making it easier to get ideas across the "abstraction
barrier" between biology and computer science, leading to more efficient and
effective bidirectional exchange of ideas between researchers and practitioners
in the field.

skill in educational contexts, leading to
creativity, and a love of learning. And while many school systems increasingly
undercut curiosity by teaching to the test, teachers are increasingly
interested in how to evoke curiosity in their students to prepare them for a
world in which lifelong learning and reskilling will be more and more
important. One aspect of curiosity that has received little attention, however,
is the role of peers in eliciting curiosity. We present an experiment in which
we have students study topics either individually or in small groups, with
subsequent assessments to evaluate how much students want to learn more about the
topic in question. We find that group learning increases curiosity 25% and
explaine this effect in terms of the central tendency bias of the average and
altered loss functions that result from social comparison.
  We further investigate why learning in groups leads to increased curiosity,
and experimentally test three mechanisms: (1) that of the average, already
discussed; (2) a mechanism of social identity, in which exposure to others'
excitement about the topic "infects" the learner with excitement about the
topic; and (3) a mechanism of competition, in which learners are motivated to
stand out from others in terms of knowledge. We find little evidence for the
last of these mechanisms, but strong evidence for that of the average.
  Finally, we experimentally test whether groups can be made more effective by
adding a social comparison dimension to the learning dimension (i.e. by learning
groups compared to learning individuals and comparing learners within groups).
We find that such comparison increases curiosity even further, by as much as
50%.
  Our results demonstrate the large effect that peers can have on curiosity and
how easily this effect can be scaled up to large learning groups through simple
design changes.
  In particular, our work highlights the importance of considering the
sociality of human learners in the development of learning technologies and
curriculum design, and how learning technologies can be designed to foster
curiosity.
  It also highlights the importance of specifying the mechanisms of effect of
different design features, so that practitioners can make informed design
decisions and build on prior research.
  Lastly, we point out how the methods we use to measure curiosity can be
applied more generally to evaluate the effectiveness of any technology or
curriculum designed to promote curiosity.

available when the input space is Euclidean, the choice is much more limited

trained using standard methods, such as inducing points. This enables graph
Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be employed in mini-batch and non-conjugate
settings, thereby extending the reach of Gaussian process models on graphs to
include scenarios in which they are needed most - when the input space is
high-dimensional.

inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourcing data from massive
urban travelers (e.g., Google Map). These data have the drawbacks of high
costs, limited coverage, or low reliability due to insufficient user

sensing, which leverages large-scale ridesourcing vehicles (RVs) to monitor and
infer the states of urban road networks. With RV traversing over road networks,
we examine the RV fleet sensing performance based on the unique number of road
segments explicitly visited, the sensing reliability as a result of repeated
visits, and the information that can be implicitly inferred given explicit data
and road network topology. We propose an optimization model to minimize the
implicit information entropy of monitoring, which is a function of both the
explicit and implicit information. The model is solved efficiently using a
decomposable algorithm. Subsequent simulations and case studies validate the
effective use of large-scale RVs in monitoring urban road networks, with the
implicit information entropy reduced by up to 27.5% compared to previous
studies. The findings of this study provide a unique sensing opportunity for
multiple civic agencies and contribute to the development of a more accurate
and reliable urban transportation system, eventually leading to a more
efficient and effective urban transportation policy.

life-changing decisions ranging from college applications to visa approvals.

than human grader, but they are still a black box to the people who are
affected by them. Research in requirements engineering and, in
natural language processing, have recently attempted small-scale and methodological
studies to understand and interpret deep learning based scoring algorithms.

work to be done to understand deep scoring systems. In this paper, we take one
small step in this direction by using few-shot learning experiments to
understand the language generalization of deep scoring models. Our key findings

  This article describes our type-based static verification tool HELMHOLTZ for
Michelson, which is a statically typed stack-based language for writing smart
contracts that are executed on the blockchain platform Tezos. HELMHOLTZ is
designed on top of our previous type system BANANAS for Michelson. BANANAS is
capable of capturing the runtime properties of programs that consume memory
allocated from the heap. In contrast, most of the previous works on type systems
only consider stack-based languages where memory is allocated from the stack.
BANANAS is the first type system capturing both heap and stack allocations in
programming languages supported by a verified compiler. HELMHOLTZ refines
BANANAS to Michelson, and is implemented as a plugin for the verifier
ssreflect-helm. HELMHOLTZ verifies the type safety of Michelson programs, and
also supports various advanced type systems such as constant propagation and
range analysis. The latter verifiers ensure that many errors, e.g., division by
zero and out-of-bounds memory accesses, that occur in practice are rejected by
the type system.
  We also present a few novel type systems for verifiable memory management in
programming languages lower than Michelson, including one for our purpose-built
RISC assembly language x86-64.
  All of the type systems have been implemented as plugins for the verifier
ssreflect-helm, and have been used to verify various example programs and
benchmarks, including the sorting program quicksort and the compiler front-end
Futhark's back-end for x86-64 assembly, leading to verifications taking anywhere
from few seconds to few minutes, respectively few hours, depending on the
complexity of the programs and the performance of the verifiers.
  Finally, we propose a general framework for verifiable memory management in
programming languages, based on our work on type systems for verifiable memory
management in programming languages supported by a verified compiler.

  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it

natural deduction. Therefore, the merit of logical pseudocodes is that every
imperative algorithm has a corresponding proof of termination of the algorithm
