Japaridze's computability logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08} is the first logic of
compositional recursive programing. It has many interesting features, e.g.,
minimal and symmetric syntax of composition (called {\it binders}), rich
semantics of programs as proofs of termination (correct and constructive over
the possible runs), higher-order programs, automatic memory management via
monads, etc. However, it has a drawback: complicated proof theory (many proof
rules and complicated proof construction). We say that a proof theory is
_minimal_ if it has few proof rules and reasonable proof construction. A proof
theory is _symmetric_ if the rules for composition (binders) for functional
programs are similar to those for non-functional programs (which use basic
commands like assignment and skip). The aim of this paper is to explore two
extensions of computability logic for even more rich programing capabilities:
threading (for programs that run many threads) and arrays (for programs that
use arrays as data structures). The definitions of computability logic for
threading and arrays are by standard reductions to its monadic version for
threading and data type definition for arrays. We present proof-out-of-witness
procedures for some basic thread and array programs, demonstrate how to write
programs by using the proofs backwards, and present two examples

for solving discrete
stochastic pursuit-evasion games (PEGs) in large grid worlds. With a partition
of the grid world into superstates (e.g., "rooms"), the proposed approach
creates a two-resolution decision-making process, which consists of a set of
local PEGs at the original state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate
level. Having much smaller cardinality, both the two sets of games can be
efficiently solved using well-known algorithms. The decision-making process
starts from solving the aggregated PEG at the superstate level to obtain a
coarse strategy, which is then used to compute a local policy for the local
PEGs at the original state level. Consequently, the proposed framework exploits
the restricted connectivity (i.e., communication/observation) of the grid
world to narrow down the competition among evaders, thus significantly reducing
the probability of pursuit failure. We prove that if the local PEGs are
solved optimally, then there exists a finite time after which a pursuit will
 succeed regardless of the players' randomized strategy. Furthermore, we show
that the tighter the superstates' partition, the smaller the aforementioned
finite time will be. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the
proposed framework in both random and semi-random environments.

remarkable success in dialog understanding tasks. However, current contrastive
learning solely considers the self-augmented dialog samples as positive samples

all possible dialogs that share similar STSs and only push away other
completely different dialogs during supervised contrastive pre-training. To
fully exploit unlabeled dialogs, a basic threshold-based score function is
used during unsupervised contrastive pre-training. Experimental results on
popular dialog understanding benchmarks show that our approach achieves
significant improvements (up to +7.1% F1 score) over strong baselines.

dynamical systems. In this article, we take a brief review of invariant sets.
We provide some results regarding the existence of invariant lines and

  Invariant sets play a significant role in the stability analysis of dynamical
systems. An invariant set is a set such that the dynamical map leaves the set
invariant, i.e., the image of the set under the map is itself. Invariant
manifolds are special types of invariant sets. They play important roles in
the reduction of the phase space of a system resulting in the formation of
normal forms. Invariant sets have significant importance in the stability
analysis of systems. Identifying the invariant sets provides valuable information
about the attractivity or repelativity of the equilibrium points, both
asymptotic and non-asymptotic, of the system. Invariant sets may contain the
equilibrium points of the system, thus determining the structure of the phase
portrait of the system. Invariant cycles are important in the context of
chaotic systems, their existence indicates the occurrence of chaos in the
system. Invariant circles are the simplest types of invariant curves in
discrete time systems. Invariant tori are important in the context of normal
form systems, their existence indicates the occurrence of quasi-periodic
dynamics in the system. Invariant manifolds are important in the context of
normal form systems. They provide a reduced representation of the phase space of
a system, obtained by approximating the invariant tori with lower dimensional
manifolds. Invariant sets play important roles in the applications of control and
synchronization of chaotic systems. A small perturbation in the parameter of a
chaotic system may result in the shifting of the invariant curve (in discrete
time systems) or manifold (in continuous time systems), leading to the
synchronization of the system.
  In this article, we provide a brief review of invariant sets. We provide the
conditions for the invariance of linear subspaces in fractional order systems.
Further, we provide an important result showing the nonexistence of invariant
manifolds (other than linear subspaces) in fractional order systems.

optimization problem is formulated to minimize the total time overhead of the

problem. Simulation results show that, compared with the conventional
exhaustive search, our proposed scheme can reduce the time overhead by as much

spectra for resolving additional scattering screens and studying their evolution

annotated training images. We introduce UniToPatho, an annotated dataset of
9536 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained patches extracted from 292 whole-slide
images, meant for training deep neural networks for colorectal polyps
classification and adenomas grading. We present our dataset and provide
insights on how to tackle the problem of automatic colorectal polyps
characterization.

datasets using common segmentation and classification architectures. Our
experiments show that segmentation and classification are strongly related,
as improving one yields an improvement in the other. We release our fully
documented dataset, with annotations and training and testing protocols, with
the aim of promoting further research in the area and helping in the direction
of the development of an end-to-end automatic characterization system, from
whole-slide image to a characterization report.
  We believe that our dataset UniToPatho to be of particular interest for the
scientific community, as it is annotated with a detailed additional tissue
description, following the Paris system for breast imaging, tailored for
colorectal polyps characterization. This rich annotation allows to study
state-of-the-art models in the task of tissue classification, as well as to
study techniques for backtracking annotations to the original whole slide
images.

evaluating the quality of the annotations with respect to the ground truth.

shadowing and edge diffraction. We obtain highly accurate solutions both
inside and outside the inhomogeneity, with a cost inferior to the classical
finite-difference methods. For example, on a homogeneous domain $[0,1]^3$ of
unit size, our method allows to reach a similar accuracy with $10^4$ unknowns
(where the time-harmonic wave equation is discretized using a classical

accurate predictions of the associated sound field in the near-field and
farrow-field, including regions of shadow and edge diffraction.

simulations and evaluated in several applications (e.g., sound reflections in
buildings, automotive design), thus showing the practical relevance of the
proposed algorithm.

problems having an infinite domain along two dimensions (e.g., $(0,\infty)^2$).

2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over unstructured meshes becomes
comparable to the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction computation.
The performance of our algorithm is demonstrated numerically on several
typical computational geometry scenarios.
  From the numerical point of view, the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.12062
contains a high-order algorithm for computing exterior harmonic functions over
general domains, which is an essential ingredient of our method. There, a
completely equivalent algorithm is derived and implemented for the case of an
inside source. When an outside source is placed on the negative x-axis, both
algorithms coincide.
  The paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.12062 contains a comparison with the
FMM-based near field computation. There, the speed-up achieved with our method
for a particular computational geometry scenario is measured over a range of
mesh sizes spanning from very fine to very coarse. The result shows a constant
speed-up of a factor 4, independent of the mesh size.
  Our high-order boundary integral algorithm for computing exterior harmonic
functions over general domains has been implemented in a C++14 based High-Order
Finite Element code, called HFELib, available at
https://github.com/hfelin/HFELib. A Python interface to easily launch simulations
and postprocess data has also been implemented using the popular
https://pyvista.pyviz.org/ library. Both the C++14 and Python implementations
include examples to solve various Laplace problems using either the direct
high-order method presented in this paper or a corresponding third order
iterative method.
